FITZPATRICK (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 51) respecting- contracts for government works. He said : This and two other Bills on the order paper in the names of Messrs. Emraerson and Hyman are practically to the same effect. The intention is to' provide that hereafter contracts in which the amount involved exceeds $5,000 will be let, not only af ter tenders have been called for, but also after they have had the sanction of the Governor General in Council. Hitherto the practice has been for the minister at the head of the department interested to dispose of such contracts. My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) will remember that in 1880 an Order in Council was passed authorizing the letting without tender of small contracts in which the amounts involved did not exceed $5,000. After I became Minister of Justice, I came to the conclusion that there was no warrant for such a proceeding. and in 1903 introduced a Bill to give legal effect to the practice. The intention now is to provide that when a contract involves expenditure of more than $5,000 it cannot be awarded by the minister alone, but must receive the sanction of the Governor General in Council.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Hon CHARLES FITZPATRICK (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 52) to amend the Franchise Act, 1898.' He said: This Bill is'to facilitate proceedings in contested election cases. The effect of it will be to enable any list of electors bearing the imprint of the King's Printer to be produced in court as prima facie evidence of the original list. At the present time, in order to prove in a contested election case that the petitioner is a qualified voter, it is necessary to do one of two things, either to summon the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to appear before the court with the original list, or to get from him a certified copy of the list. Either method is cumbrous and expensive, and to overcome the difficulty this amendment is proposed.
Motion agreed to. and Bill read the first time.

Hon. CHARLES HYMAN (Acting Minister of Public Works) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 54) to amend the Public Works Act. He said : The purpose of this Bill is explained by the statement of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) concerning the Act respecting contract for government works.

How will that affect the practice, which was in vogue in 1890 at least, of giving work out without tender or doing it by day labour if it did not exceed $5,000 ? Is that excepted now under this Bill ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: These Bills do not affect that question. That was affected by the Bill of 1903. As I said a moment ago, my hon. friend will remember that in 1880 an Order in Council was passed authorizing the Minister of Public Works to let contra els for works that did not exceed $5,000 without tender or by private tender. I came to the conclusion that there was not statutory authority for that practice, and it was doubtful whether the Order in Council was effective. And, in order to make it effective I introduce the legislation of 1893.
So that works below $5,000 could be carried out in tin's way ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

There is an ingenious way of getting around that provision, by cutting the work up in sections of $5,000 of less and spending, it may be $30,000 or $40,000 in the end. That is very much like an evasion of the spirit of the Act, and ought to be provided against in some way. I know that it is a little difficult because the minister may say : What I propose to do amounts to $5,000 or less, but when that is done, his intentions may broaden and he may want another $5,000 worth done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it is the intention of the House-and after all this legislation is intended to give effect to the intention of the House-that a contract that involves $5,000 or more shall not be let except by public tender. Still, of couse, we know there are works of immediate pressing necessity that must be done without tender. When the Bill is in committee, I shall be glad to consider any amendment that will make in the direction of requiring public tenders for contracts of over $5,000.
As I understand it, it is not so much the intention to interfere with the present law as to take the jurisdiction from the department and give it to the Governor in Council.

But the department, apparently may carry on a work involving more than that $5,000 where there is no contract at all. Are they not building the Mr. FITZPATRICK.

I wish to call the attention of the House to what is, in my estimation at least, an interference by the government with proceedings actually going on in Quebec. A political crisis has arisen in the provincial cabinet, and we are entitled here, as members of the House, to know exactly what part the government of Canada is taking in that crisis. I mentioned a moment ago that within the last ten days we have had here from Quebec interviewing the right hon. gentleman and other members of the government, ministers of the cabinet in the province of Quebec who have not resigned, and we have had others up here on alternate days who have resigned. We have had a large number of members of this House and of members of the cabinet moving down to Quebec, and down to Montreal, in connection with this crisis. Liberal organs announced freely before the opening of the session that my right lion, friend himself liad gone down to Quebec, and made no secret of the object of his mission; he had gone down there in order to set matters right, and arrange the internal difficulties that have arisen in the cabinet itself at Quebec. The government organ in the city of Montreal, the Montreal ' Herald,' states this in regard to the point which I have just raised. It contains a telegram from Quebec dated February 9.
Conciliation was in the air all day. Hon. L. P. Brodeur and Senator Dandurand were on hand as peace makers and they did their best.
Further on :

It was obvious an hour after breakfast time, that there was ' something doing.' Mr. Brodeur had come in by the morning train. Mr. Dandurand was stopping with relatives. Presently it was whispered that these gentlemen, acting at Sir Wilfrid Laurier's request, were doing their best to make peace. In the course of the day

the ex-ministers had several interviews with Hon. Mr. McCorkill and Hon. Mr. Archambatilt.
It is conceded by all who have been in any way privy to what went on that, in a day of disappointments, the one clear gain to the party is a pronounced enhancement of Mr. MeCorkill's reputation as a public man.
I could quote from several of the Liberal organs' articles, telegrams and items which point clearly to the interference of this government and by members of the government with the difficulties which have arisen at Quebec and which are very far from a solution as my right lion, friend knows better than any one else. On two occasions the attention of the government has been called to this point. Yesterday my lion, friend from Laval (Hr. Leonard) knowing, as everybody knew, it. being a matter of public notoriety that the lion. Minister of Inland Revenue had gone down to Quebec with the mission with which lie was charged as has been intimated here by the Montreal ' Herald,' asked that we should have some report. Ministers are responsible to the House of Commons in general and they are responsible for every one of their acts. As I understood the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) lie stated that the hon. Minister of Inland Itevenuo was absent at Quebec and instead of listening to vague rumours of all sorts, my hon. friend would receive to-day some answer, some information from that minister. The hon. Minister of Inland Revenue has been in the House since three o'clock. He has, as has been noticed by everybody made a report evidently of bis mission to Quebec to a number of hon. members of this House, and 1 think it is only fair to us to-day in view of the promise made yesterday that he should tell us what the mission was with which he was charged and with what results he has performed the mission.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that I cannot gratify the very fastidious curiosity of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). I wisii I could. The ideas of my hon. friend and my ideas in regard to responsible government do not agree. There is a crisis in Quebec. It is not the first time that there have been crises in governments ; it has happened before and perhaps may happen again so long as men are men and divide into opposite parties. My hon. friend said that he wanted to know what part the government intend to take or are taking in regard to the crisis at Quebec. I am very glad that I can satisfy him on that point. The government are taking no part whatever in the crisis at Quebec and the government have no part to take in that crisis. I do not deny that personally I am very much concerned in what is taking place at Quebec. I take an interest in what is going on, some of my colleagues do the same and I understand also
that on the other side of the House a very deep interest is taken in that crisis. My hon. friend is not perhaps the least of those who take an interest in it. Perhaps he is not as immediately concerned as I am, because the crisis is not amongst his own political friends, but in the charity of liis bosom he takes an interest in it as if it were amongst his own friends. I have to say that if my colleague, Mr. Brodeur, went to Quebec, he went simply as Mr. Brodeur and in no other capacity. My hon. friend! says that ministers are responsible for their actions. There is no doubt that ministers are responsible for their actions when they act as members of the government in matters which concern the government, but if a minister of the Crown goes to Quebec or Montreal, I do not think he gives an account where he sleeps or what he has done or how he has disposed of his time. I think that as much libertv ought to be given a minister as any other man. If because a man is a member of the government does it follow that he must be dogged and followed and that he shall give an account of what he has done during his trip ?
The defence of my hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has certainly not been a very long one and I think the House will agree with me that it has not been a very strong one.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, because there is nothing to defend.

I do not think that any one will stand up and say that it has been a very skilful one or a very frank one. It is impossible that the whole public sentiment of the country can be under a grave mistake in believing that there is an attempt being made by the government here in Ottawa, or certain of its individual members, to interfere in the party crisis which has taken place in the province of Quebec. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) has quoted original extracts from one of my right hon. friends own well-informed papers. Neither the editor of that paper nor the staff of reporters who work for that paper are without sense or intelligence, and it is impossible that these things would be going on and be reported as they are by my right hon. friend's own papers in plain and unmistakable terms if there was not something in them. Does my right hon. friend think that what he has stated here to-day will disarm public sentiment and operate the impression that he and the members of his government are taking no interest at all in this crisis at Quebec ? I do not think so. and I do not believe there is a man in this House who reasonably looks upon the thing who will come to that conclusion either. The hon. Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Brodeur) left his place and went down with that alter ego of the right hon. gentleman in matters political. Senator Dandurand,

There is an additional reason why the House is interested in this case. Not only has a minister of the Crown gone from here to do conciliatory work but he is accompanied by the Speaker of the Senate ; both branches of the legislature have been pressed into service to do political work down there. Heretofore it has always been claimed that the upper House had no politics ; there were no political shadows there, the Senate was quite independent That was the Reform doctrine but now even the first man in the Senate, the hon. the Speaker of the Senate, is pressed into service along with a minister of the Crown to go down there and patch up some kind of an arrangement between the present leader of the provincial government and the other ministers who are rebelling against him.
That being the case, it seems to me that we are specially interested to know whether we are drifting. If members of both Houses of parliament are going to be forced to take part as politicians in these provincial feuds and troubles, the affairs of the provinces and the affairs of the Dominion are not going to be kept as distinct as we were led to believe, from the professions of hon. gentlemen opposite hitherto, would be the case.

(Translation). Mr. Speaker, I heard with pleasure tha Right Hon. Prime Minister state that he had given no instructions to the Hon. Minister of Inland Revenue. I am bound to accept his word ; but,-always in connection with that crisis at Quebec- may I inquire of the right hon. gentleman whether he has read an article of the * So-leil ', dated February 8, in respect to the policy followed by that paper. speechtext:
The stand taken by the ' Soleil,' during the present crisis, is variously appreciated. Those whose life-long weakness has been to talk too much could not very well miss this opportunity of falling into their capital sin.
Tn set things right, we may state once for all that the ' Soleil ' is the organ of the Liberal party, and as such, under the absolute guidance and control of Sir Wilfrid. Consequently, the partisans of Sir Wilfrid, those who are sincerely so, as well as those who call themselves such, will please take note of the fact.
If the above editorial states the truth, I am unable to understand how the Right Hon. Prime Minister can inform the House that he does not interfere with Quebec politics.
Then I read on the same page of the ' Soleil ' another article under the following heading :
Now that the first moment of excitement is over, light is dawning again, and the true

question at issue, as laid down by us yesterday, is very clearly in evidence.
It was necessary that a number of honest minded people living in far off counties, and who had been made to believe in the existence of a political scandal, should have their minds disabused as soon as possible. It cannot be said too many times, and it is an actual truth, that the whole matter is a question of personal differences and personal dislikes.
The ' Evenement ' is, therefore, completely at variance with the facts when it points to recent events as a vindication of the criticism made and the charges brought forth for the last five years by the party to which it belongs. Such an accusation, the Liberal party cannot afford to assent to, unless they wish to shamefully repudiate themselves.
It is the Parent government and no other which has been entrusted with the task of managing public affairs. Should there be any doubt as to the truth of this contention, it would be necessary in order to disprove It, to make a new appeal to the people. It is the rank and file who undergo the hazards of war, but it is the general who gets the credit for any success. The victories won by the Liberal party in 1900 and 1904 are in justice attributable to the Hon. S. N. Parent. As Scipio Africanus, he might proudly say to his accusers : ' Twice have I led you to victory, now let us proceed to the Capitol to thank the gods.' And it shall be in order to follow him.
If ever time was ill chosen to remove a leader is it not just now, hardly three months after the most overwhelming victory which ever a party has had to its credit ?
The Liberal party has come out of it so powerful as to become headstrong, believing that it can with impunity indulge all its fancies, even to the point of revelling in internal strifes for the mere pleasure of a change. But those are untoward fancies, the result of thoughtlessness. Once the first nervous crisis has been got over, wisdom will assert its rights, and it will be conceded that the least that could be expected by a political leader, after fifteen years of services of an exceptionally fruitful nature to the country, is to be allowed to depart with full honours. To attempt to remove him by sheer force would be acting contrary to common sense. It would be putting him fully in the right, and the people completely in the wrong.
Such is the question, rid of all unpleasantness, and as the representatives of the people in this province should look at it to-day.
Has that article been written at the request or at the suggestion of the Right Hon. Prime Minister ?
Is it true the lion. Minister of Inland Revenue has' just returned to Quebec ?

speechtext: That is the first news I have had of it.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of the premier a question to which he promised me a reply in a few days ; I also wish to bring it to the attention of the lion.

Postmaster General. The question which is one of very serious interest to my province, refers to the communication at present maintained between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. As I explained yesterday, it is now7 carried on by iceboats, and when the iceboats reach the main land at Cape Tormentine, there is no special train to carry the mails to Sackville, a distance of 35 miles. This is a great hardship. Hon. members have only to go to the reading room to see that the last papers received from Prince Edward Island are nearly a week old. Any one can imagine what the business men of the province suffer in this matter. I am instructed by a telegram from my province, which I will read to the House :
Before the orders of the day, interrogate the premier every day about island communication.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Name, name.

That is a very hard duty imposed upon me, to stand up every day and interrogate the government about the communication with Prince Edward Island. I think the only thing they can do is to remedy this grievance, and thus relieve me of a very unpleasant duty and at the same time do justice to the province.

Mr. Speaker, I am extremely sorry that the state of the climate or the weather has interrupted communication between the mainland and Prince Edward Island. This is not the first time that there has been such interruption. I wish I could hope that it will be the last.
Change the government.

It was worse under the late regime. I can remember in the days that are beyond recall, when a good representative of Prince Edward Island, Mr. Perry, like my kon. friend, announced to parliament how Providence, in view of the government of the day, was smiting Prince Edward Island, as it seems to be doing in a lesser degree to-day, the government of that day did not put on special trains, or even special ships. They allowed the people to get across in small ferry boats and to carry the mails as best they could, very frequently at the peril of their lives. We have endeavoured to improve the service as much as possible, and this year we have two steamers endeavouring to keep open communication. If the floating ice has made'it impossible for these steamers to navigate, I suppose the only solution would be to get more powerful steamers, perhaps ice breakers such as are used in Russia. That would be a very considerable expense. I do not say the government would not be justified in undertaking it, but there can be no satisfactory and uninterrupted communication between the Island and the mainland until some means

are devised for overcoming the difficulty of floating ice that becomes congested in the channel. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice has made a suggestion to me that would perhaps commend itself to my hon. friend. The difficulty arises from vis major -something beyond the control of the government. .

Vis inertiae.
Sir AVILLIAiM MULOCK. No, the vis inertiae was in the olden days.
There are some tilings that you forget.

There are some things the hon. member for North Toronto forgets, and it would be well to remind him of some of his history. He is a public man with a past. However, I am dealing with the present now. My hon. friend from Queen's (Mr. Martin) is seeking for information in obedience to the mandate of his correspondent, to worry the House each day, in the hope that, like the unjust judge, we may at last yield to his importunity. However, Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that we could not establish the precedent of employing special trains to meet every interruption of the mail service. That has never been done, and I doubt if any government would be willing deliberately to undertake it. Therefore, to resume the train of my thoughts when they were interrupted by the hon. friend for North Tor-oronto
Very mean thoughts, too.
What does the hon. gentleman mean ?
I will tell him when he gets through.

I certainly am utterly at a loss as to the meaning of the hon. gentleman, but if he wants time to invent some substance for what he says, I have no objection. I was going to suggest that this House is not the tribunal which can overcome the operations of nature. We certainly cannot overcome the congestion of ice, and I cannot hold out any hope of the government subsidizing special trains to carry the mails. We endeavour to utilize all the regular trains which the companies choose to establish, and even if they were to put on special trains for other purposes, I am sure we would be glad to use them ; but as to the department subsidizing special trains to carry the mails, I would hesitate before inaugurating any such policy.

The hon. gentleman has, as usual, been giving free rein to his imagination, and the length to which that imagination can carry him is immeasurable. He conjured up a condition of things which never had any existence, and which he must know was purely imaginary. He painted 27
that imaginary condition in vivid colours, and then endeavoured to show by contrast how much better he and his government had done. But there never was a time under the late administration when we depended) on ferry boats to carry on navigation be-( tween Prince Edward Island and the main-1 land.
Yes, there was.

There never was a time in the late administration when that was done ; but, of course, if the hon. gentleman wants to go back to pioneer times, he will find that at one period the only communication between the island and the mainland was by canoe.
I am referring to a time when the hon. gentleman was in this House.
The hon. gentleman is utterly at sea. He is in the habit of drawing on his imagination
It is a fact.

He is in the habit of painting an imaginary condition and then using that as a foil to show how much better things are done now. The people of Prince Edward Island have a perfect right to ventilate their grievance. When their facilities of travel are interrupted, they have a perfect right to ask their representative to plead their case before the government. But when they do so they receive but scant sympathy or mercy from this administration. In fact, some hon. gentlemen on that side were good enough to suggest that the constituents of my hon. friend should get up and use their shovels to clear away the railway tracks. I believe it was the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
It was the Minister of Railways (Mr. Emmerson).

That shows you how the Liberal party regards the grievances of the people. It is the old story. All they look at is what will benefit the party. The hon. gentleman was good enough to say that I was a man with a past. Has he a past ? Who does not remember ; who that was here in the days before 1806, does not re-' member how my hon. friend, in the long weary years when he was in opposition, was a prominent figure, and not a very creditable one in many ways, in this House ? Who does not remember how he looked up at the galleries and swore eternal opposition on any kind of a salary like $50,000 for the Governor General ? Can any one fail to recollect how he tried to make capital with the farmers by posing as a patron and introducing a Bill providing that no member of this parliament should have a pass and travel upon railways by the favour ana option of the railway companies ? Who



does not remember how he advocated economies which he has since repudiated V Why did he do this ? Either because he was honest and had convictions, or because he was seeking to deceive the public with the object of gaining their votes and getting into power. Well, he got into power, and what happened ? Do we not all remember how eloquent he was in opposition against members sitting in this House with promises of offices and emoluments in then- pockets V So far did his convictions carry him that he introduced a Bill to make it impossible for any one who had been a member of this House to obtain an office of emolument of any kind until he had been a certain number of years out of parliament. Yet that gentleman, who tells us that he nas no past, and who twits another hon. member with his past, sat in this House through two terms of parliament after 1896-the year the present government - took office-and when he had come to the end of the two terms, he had before his eyes a list of fifty members of parliament and seuators who had, in the course of these two years, been given offices of emolument by this government and had sat and voted in this House with promises of these in their trousers' pockets. Who does not remember the gentleman from Quebec who sat yonder with a promise from the First Minister of either a lieutenant governorship or a judgeship of a higher court in the province of Quebec in his pocket, voting for measures which, in his heart, he did not believe in, and which, with his lips, he said he did not believe in, but for which he voted because of the promise he held in his pocket ? That was wrong in itself, but, worse yet, the fulfilment of that promise was kept back by the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues for one and a half or two years, in order that they might still keep that supporter in his seat. The hon. gentleman thinks there are some things we would like to forget, and twits us with wishing to forget them. He may forget for himself a display of lack of conviction, want of sincerity and disregard of principles, which is without precedent in the public records of this country.
Sir WILLIAM MULOCIv. As the hon. member for North Toronto has spoken twice on this motion, perhaps the House will be similarly indulgent in my regard. Of course, my hon. friend must be allowed some latitude. and it reminds one of olden times to see him take his stand and, witli that digit finger of his, threaten any one against whom he directs his spleen and disappointment. He. of course, may claim some indulgence. If I had it in my composition-and I thank God I have not-to nurse during four years feelings of animosity and take the first opportunity to give vent to them, I might follow the example of my hon. friend, and, on each occasion when I rise to address the House, endeavour to misrepresent and tor-Mr. FOSTER.
ture the record of those to whom I am opposed and excite heart-burnings and vengeful feelings among them. My hon. friend has sought to vent his disappointment on my head by going back into the past. But if I should look up his past. I hardly think it would prove very edifying. I can well remember the platform upon which he secured an entry into political life, and how well he wriggled away from that platform, when he said that if it did happen that at one time he had committed himself to the doctrine of prohibition, that was only in a moment of weakness. After he had started on his public career and won his spurs and his position in__this House as an advocate of that doctrine, after he had delivered in this House philippic after philippic to show his zeal for the cause, no sooner did he get into office than he apologized for his mistake and pleaded infancy as his excuse. Well, I am willing to forget his boyhood days and throw the mantle of charity over them, but there are some events of more recent date, in which the hon. gentleman was a prominent figure, and with regard to which he cannot plead the same excuse. He could hardly plead weakness and infancy and inexperience, or even temporary insanity, for what occurred in 1896.
And what occurred ? I remember well occupying at that time the seat now occupied by my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Morin). The hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) was sitting where the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) sits to-day. There was an histrionic incident in the month of January, 1896, when the ex-premier. Sir Mackenzie Bowell, coming forward to the floor of this House as the Speaker left the "chair, stated that for six months he had been sitting witli the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) and others whom he described as a nest of traitors with the hon. gentleman as their leader. He selected the hon. gentleman as the most distinguished member of that body and said that for six months that gentleman, if he might so describe him, had been endeavouring to cut his throat. What are their relations to-day, between the former prime minister (Sir Mackenzie Bowel] i and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster)? Has the hon. gentleman received absolution from Sir Mackenzie ? Has he made amends to him ? Has he ever yet given to the public an explanation and defence of that transaction ? Why, I read in the press during the last campaign that, in North Toronto-1! think it was North Toronto-the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) was asked to explain and justify his conduct as a public man in having betrayed his leader, and having caused a strike among his friends to prevent that leader from re-forming the government. He was asked to explain and to justify, if he could, his treachery on that occasion. And what did he say ? He said that his mouth was sealed ; that he had given his explanation to His Excellency and he was satis-

fied. There was courage for you. The hon. gentleman showed the high quality of his courage by taking shelter for an indefensible transaction behind His Excellency the Governor of Canada.
And what would my hon. friend (Sir William Mulock) have done ?

I certainly trust I would not have been guilty-as I think no hon. gentleman would ever be guilty-of the offence of my hon. friend. He is teaching us what our political morals ought to be. But what did he himself do? Sir Mackenzie Bowell was a member of parliament long before the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) entered this House. He was taken into the government of Sir .Tohn Macdonald in 1878. He was Sir John Macdonald's trusted colleague for many years. In 18S3 or 1885, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) became a colleague of Sir Mackenzie Bowell under Sir John Macdonald. He sat with Sir Mackenzie Bowell in Council from the time he joined the cabinet until the lamented death of Sir John Thompson. He had ten- years association with him in the Council chamber as well in the party organization. And, when it became necessary to appoint a premier in the month of January, or thereabouts, 1895, the hon. gentleman (Mr.'Foster) I presume, joined with others in recommending Sir Mackenzie Bowell. He took office under him and served under him-if service it can be called-for a year. He waited until parliament met on the 2nd of January, 1896. After the speech from the Throne had been delivered and the House had assembled to receive that speech, instead of moving in a manly way that the speech should be taken into consideration the next day the hon. gentleman moved for some reason mysterious at the time but afterwards made clear-that the House should stand adjourned until the following Tuesday. Saturday came and then the conspiracy was laid bare before the public, and, for two weeks the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) took up his position in room 16, he and a few more, to prevent Sir Mackenzie Bowell re-forming his cabinet. He endeavoured by the arts of the striker to destroy constitutional government and betray his chief. The hon. gentleman now asks me what I would have done. I ask him if he can find any parallel for his conduct in any parliamentary body ? You will search in vain the history of constitutional government 'jn Great Britain and its colonies to find a precedent for such a transaction.
What about Quebec today ?	'

I am dealing with my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster). He has asked me to refer to his history, and I am doing so. He refers to me, and he is quite at liberty to refer to me. He mentions certain propositions of 271	.
mine in days gone by. He knows perfectly well that it is one thing for a member to have individual views, but that it is quite another thing for him to impress those views upon his colleagues. It is true, since he alludes to it-though I never publicly made an observation upon the subject-that I did not approve, so far as I myself was concerned, of a member of parliament travelling upon a railway pass. I never said so before -never expressed an opinion upon the subject. I do not propose to lay down a rule of conduct for the guidance of my fellow-men. They are the keepers of their consciences, as 1 am the keeper of mine. I have entertained that view and have lived up to it strictly throughout the whole of my public career. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) means to insinuate to the contrary, he is not correct in his insinuation. At present the law provides that members of parliament are entitled to travel free. I am under no obligation to any railway company if I travel free now in Canada, for it is my legal right to do so. Moreover if I had used a railway pass every day since I became Postmaster General I should have been within my legal rights, for it is provided in the contract between the railways and the department that the Postmaster General is entitled so to travel. However, I have not happened to make use of that provision. I did not exercise my right in that particular until parliament had placed upon the statute-book a law vesting that right in members of parliament. The hon. gentleman- says I supported a measure to prevent members of parliament being appointed to office. It is true that in the year, 1895, I introduced a Bill of that kind. When I introduced it the only person in parliament, who made the slightest inquiry of me as to its meaning was my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster). He asked me to explain the Bill. I explained it. He with a very contemptible nod of his head, said, ' that's all.' And that is all he had to say in the way of expressing an opinion on the subject. No member of parliament expressed approval of the Bill, and I am not aware that the sentiments I gave expression to were shared by any member of parliament then or are shared by any member of parliament now. So, what was the use of my pressing an opinion that had no support in parliament, or, apparently out of parliament. There is such a thing as having views, but there is also such a thing as having to submit to the views of others; and, in this age and in the way we do business in this country and elsewhere, organization is essential to accomplish anything in life. If my hon. friend desires to discuss other features of my public life. I am quite prepared to meet him. But, before concluding I would ask him again if he would give the country an explanation-and justification, if he can-of his action in 1896 in betraying his leader, Sir Mackenzie Bowell. He knew that gentleman for 20 years, he was his

colleague for ten years, he enlisted under and served under him, he took the oath of allegiance to him, that he would be loyal-
Where ?
Does not a gentleman who takes office bind himself in honour to
The hon. gentleman (Sir William Mulock) said he took the oath of allegiance to him.
That is his imagination.

Does bethink he is living up to his oath of office as a member of the cabinet if the gentleman betrays the premier? However, the matter is before the hon. gentleman. Since he has asked me to discuss his history, I give him this opportunity; now to justify to the country, if he can, his action on that occasion. We are all desirous of having his explanation. We want him to tell us why, having with his friends sat for ten years in Council With Sir Mackenzie Rowell, having joined ii. the formation of his government, having served with him for all that time, he should, between the meeting of the House on Thursday and the following Tuesday, the date ot the reassembling of the House to take into consideration His Excellency's address-wo want to know why it was that he then sprang that surprise on Sir Mackenzie Bowell, and committed that act which is without a parallel in Canadian history, and I trust ever will remain without a parallel ?

It was not my intention to take part in the present debate; I would have been satisfied with the part played by my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and my hon. friend the Postmaster General. It was the Postmaster General who commenced the attack. There was no necessity at all for that speech of his, referring to the past history of my hon. friend. 'He got exactly what he deserved.

I beg yom pardon, the hon. gentleman forgets. If wo are going to extend this peculiar debate -the hon. member for North Toronto interrupted me by a very offensive observation, which -was without foundation in fact.
What was the offensive observation, I ask my hon. friend?
' Hansard ' will tell it.
The hon. gentleman does not know it.

I listened carefully to the Postmaster General's reference to my hon. friend, and I think it was totally uncalled for, and he got the dressing which he richly deserved. The hon. gentleman, foi the purpose of finishing off my hon. friend from North Toronto, refers to an episode Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
which took place in 1896 and to my hon. friend's part in that affair. He says it was a crime of which history furnishes no parallel, that nothing like it ever occurred in the history of any country before.
Do you know of any?

If the hon. gentleman knew all the facts in relation to it he would be one of the first to justify my hon. friend from North Toronto. A correct statement has never been made of that affair, but very likely it will be made shortly. You know, Mr. Speaker, the position of the Conservative party in 189G; you know the difficulties that the hon. gentleman who was at the head of the government had ini carrying on the affairs of government. There was a question which arose in reference to school affairs in the Northwest. First of all, we had a gentleman) who left the government, left his leader at that time, as the hon. gentleman says, Mr. Clarke Wallace, a member for one of the Yorks. Afterwards Mr. Angers left the government, then two other French gentlemen, Mr. Ouimet and Sir Adolphe Caron, followed suit. They all had a right to do it; they resigned from tne government for different reasons. Afterwards there was an attempt to reconstruct the government. Sir Charles Tupper was in this country. I do not know the reasons why he came out here. My own idea is that he came out at the request of Sir Mackenzie Bowell and of some of his colleagues in the government. But there was no secret about it. It was well known then that Sir Mackenzie Bowell-I have no objections to that hon. gentleman, I have the kindliest feelings for him-it was well known that the party at that time, a party which had a majority in the country in every province, was dying for lack of good management, for want of a federal leader at Ottawa. It was with the consent of Sir Mackenzie Bowell, as well as the rest of his colleagues, that Sir Charles Tupper was asked to form a government. These are the facts. All were loyal to Sir Mackenzie Bowell until it was known by his colleagues that he was a party to Sir Charles Tupper taking the leadership of the Conservative party. From day to day, from time to time, like a sick girl hanging on to life, he did not hand in his resignation as his colleagues in the cabinet expected of him. There was then no other remedy than the remedy that the Conservative leaders, or the colleagues of Sir Mackenzie Bowell, took at that time. They did it, not for themselves. My hon. friend had nothing to gain, lie was getting no promotion, nor was I. We may have been wrong, we may have made a mistake at the time, but we did it thinking it was in the best interests of the Liberal-Conservative party and for the purpose of benefiting that party. From that moment to the present day I have never felt sorry for what I did at that time. My

iion. friend performed the same act that 1 did myself, and I am confident that he did it because he thought it was in the interest of his country, or at least in the interest of the Liberal-Conservative party. There was nothing else left for us to do, and we did it. We may have done wrong, we may have done what the Postmaster General says was not the act of gentlemen. But who has constituted him an authority to say what the conduct of a gentleman should be in reference to that affair? Who has constituted him a censor of the acts of those hon. gentlemen at that time? What I say is this, and I say it for myself and my colleagues, that we acted on that occasion, as wi believed, in the interests of the country, and in the interest of the party. For those reasons I now rise for the purpose of defending my hon. friend. When the whole history of that transaction is written, there will not be a single man from one end of this country to the other who can point a finger at any of these gentlemen and charge them with having done wrong.
iMr. FOSTER. I do not know that 1 have a right to ask it, but 1 would like to say about twenty-five words in answer to my hon. friend in a very cool and collected way- not by way of recrimination. It is not an interesting thing, and probably it is not a very pleasant thing, to hurl these recriminations against one another as representatives of a party. My hon. friend opposite has followed me from that time to this with his peculiar version of the affair of 1896, not only in parliament, but to a certain extent in every contest in which I have engaged, like a sleuth hound on my, track.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Order.
I do not think that is out of order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Like a sleuth hound.
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is that the modem way?

My hon. friend knows what a hound is for. He is to track his prey by whatever instincts and capabilities Providence has endowed him with. In my contest in North Ontario, my hon. friend did me the honour to track me. He followed me from concession to concession, and his chief stock in trade was this particular version of his as to my not acting as a man and a gentleman in 1896. Now, it is just as well that I should state once and for all in parliament, very briefly, just what I did and just what I conceive I was right in doing. That is all I want to do. From that time in 1896 up to this present moment, although I have been hounded-as I have stated-I do not find fault with any one for doing that if he thinks it is a good piece of party politicsalthough it has been thrown in my teeth everywhere I have never yet stood up in public when attacked, I have never once allowed myself to give the version plain and clear of my action at that time. Why ? Because I did not think it was in the interest of the public life of this country for me to do it. I felt that I would rather take the implications and the charges and whatever penalty came with them than violate what I conceived to be a good maxim in public life, that in these matters we are bound by our oath and our position as privy councillors to give our reasons to His Excellency and to let them bide there. Now, the first charge that my hon. friend brought against me was that I came into this House on the prohibition platform and that I repudiated my principles later. This is incorrect in every particular. I came into this House and I take now the opportunity of stating that I came into this House as a teetotaler in practice, as a prohibitionist in principle, well known because these had been my principles, right or wrong from my youth up-My canvass in the county in which I won my first election was absolutely outside the question of prohibition, and there is no man in this country that can say to the contrary. My published circular to my people, my call to them and my whole canvass were on the question of the policy of the government in regard to trade matters particularly and that alone, and I came to this parliament as an independent- Conservative in favour of the National Policy. The hon. gentleman says that a man may have individual opinions, but that when he becomes a member of a government he may not be able to make his opinions effective and he excused himself in two particulars for his not having carried out as a member of the government what he held to be right as a private individual. Will not the same reasoning apply to me ?
But the hon. gentleman abjured his principles.

The hon. gentleman abjured his principles ? It does not lie in the mouth of my hon. friend to make that statement now nor did it ever. If the hon. gentleman can say that I have violated my total abstinence principles let him stand up and bring the proof. If he can say that I have violated my prohibitionist principles let him stand up and say so. I am not such a ninny or so absurd, or so wanting in common sense as to think, however strongly a man may hold individual prohibition opinions that he is able to put them upon the country unless the majority of the electors will stand behind his back. I never thought so, never said so, and never tried to. My hon. friend justifies himself by saying that he could not carry out in the government individual opinions because he could not impress them upon the majority of the government. It is within the judgment of the

House whether there has ever been a time in the history of this parliament when I or any other prohibitionist could impress our views on the majority of the House with sufficient strength as to bring about the enactment of a prohibitory law.
My hon. friend says that I was no gentleman in that I swore an oath of allegiance to my premier and broke it. I was not aware of swearing any oath of allegianc to my premier, nor do I think my hon. friend is aware of having sworn any oath of allegiance to his premier. Am I not to be allowed to leave the government if I differ from it on points of policy or principle ? Is a man to be branded as no gentleman because, differing from what is the policy and principle of his government, he leaves it ? Did not Mr. Angers, Mr. Ouimet, Sir Adolphe Caron and Mr. Clarke Wallace leave the government ? Were they no gentlemen ? There have been gentlemen who have left the government of the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). And why ? Because they differed upon points of policy and upon principle from his government. Did they violate their oaths of allegiance to the premier or were they no gentlemen because they left ? The statement of my hon. friend will not hold good in that respect. At whatever time a member of the government feels that he is out of accord with his premier and the government of which he is a member on .points of policy or administration. he has a perfect right to send in his resignation and he retains all his attributes of a gentleman and an honourable man in doing so. I did not leave the government for financial preference or personal emolument. When I left the government I left my position and I left my salary. I gave my demission in to the Governor General. I justified, as we all did, my resignation by the explanations which I made to the Governor General. I presume the Governor General who heard our explanations and received them did not apparently come to the. conclusion that we were no gentlemen or that we had violated our oaths of allegiance as was stated by my hon. friend for that very same Governor General made ns again members of the following government without stain and without reproach. Now. what does my hon. friend wish me to do ? What would he have done, I venture to ask him, if he were in the same position as I, not that I think he is apt to be in such a position ? He hangs on pretty thoroughly and pretty closely, but suppose my hon. friend came to the conclusion that he could not agree with his premier on some line of public policy, would he have violated his standard of gentlemanly conduct if he had frankly told the premier so and left ? Before I or any of my colleagues left the government, our premier knew our position and had it within his own hands. Would my hon. friend be not acting the part of a gentleman because, Mr. FOSTER.
if he disagreed with his premier to-day or to-morrow, he left the government, or, if he said : As an honest man I cannot agree with you on this question of policy or principle, and I hand in my resignation ? He will not say so. Therefore, the charge he urged against me in this respect has no force at all.
By what right did he call this a conspiracy ? Does the hon. gentleman, himself, know the circumstances of the case ? A reasonable man or a careful man will not make a statement of that kind except upon thorough knowledge. What thorough knowledge has my hon. friend of the circumstances of the case ? Has he any ? Was he within the secrets of the Council 1 Has he been made the bosom friend and confident of any member of the government of that time ? I venture to say that he has not. On what authority does he stand up here and say that this was a conspiracy, not knowing the facts of the case, not knowing a single one of the facts of the case ? So when you come to reason fairly and carefully on the premises of my hon. friend they do not hold water. So far as I am concerned that is the statement of my position. I make it here in the House and I apologize to the House for having had to take up their time to make it, but it has been often urged outside of the House and up to this time I have never taken occasion to vindicate myself by making a statement. When it was brought up and elevated to the dignity of what I might call a front bench question, I thought it was only fair for me to ask my right hon. friend and the House to indulge me in making this plain statement of the affair.

The hon. gentleman has asked me a question and I presume I shall be allowed to reply to it. I am pleased to recognize the more moderate manner in which he has endeavoured to express himself and I shall try to follow that worthy example.
That is right.
See the effect of good example and of bad example. My hon. friend asks me on what authority 1 stated that there was a conspiracy. I made the statement upon the authority of Sir Mackenzie Bowel],
None better.

Sir Mackenzie Bowell made a public statement-he did not make it to me-which appeared in the press of the day charging these gentlemen with being a nest of traitors. I do not know what authority that is but it is sufficient for me because he was the premier.
I would call attention to the violence of my hon. friend's remarks. No one questions the right of any member of a government to resign. It is his duty to resign if

lie is not in harmony with the policy of the government, but my hon. friend lias not explained this point. The question is not whether a man may or may not properly resign ; the question in this case is' to explain the coincidence of seven members of a government resigning after the House was called together, after the speech from the Throne had been presented and before it had been taken into consideration; and during the time the government was in that chaotic state these seven gentlemen using their best endeavours to prevent the leader reforming his government. These are things that have not been explained.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) made a motion today asking for two days now occupied by the private members of this House, so that we might get through with the business rapidly. The opposition cheerfully granted tlie motion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Cheerfully V My hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) did not hear my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier ('Mr. Monk).

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It was done cheerfully ; your motion carried. One day of the government has been taken up by an hon. member, friend of the government in making an attack upon the opposition which was quite unjustified.
I did not make an attack.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And in his last statement he makes a charge against Sir Mackenzie Rowell that I do not think he can justify. He said that Sir Mackenzie Rowell stated that his former colleagues were a nest of traitors.
Not all of them.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I never saw that statement published and I think the only justification he had for saying that was some words that escaped Sir Mackenzie Rowell here in this House, after the Speaker had-left the Chair, when he was in a passion. I wish to corroborate a statement of the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Hag-gart). I was then as now whip of the Conservative party. I was the go-between between Sir Mackenzie Rowell and the ministers who had left his cabinet. I had consultations with both of them. There was a deadlock ; the cabinet had resigned as they had a right to do. My hon. friend (Sir William Mu lock) has no right to charge these gentlemen with trying to prevent Sir Mackenzie Rowell from forming a cabinet I was in the confidence of both parties and it was at the request of Sir Mackenzie Rowell that I saw Sir Charles Tupper and got them together, and they arranged between themselves and made a bargain that Sir Charles Tupper
What was the bargain ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: There are two or three young members from the eastern part of the Dominion who have seen fit to-day several times to insult gentlemen on this side of the House when speaking. I will ask you, Mr. Speaker, to draw their attention to the fact that they are quite unparliamentary in their conduct.
And they are not at all discouraged by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson).
Order.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I want you to inform them-or I shall through you-that it is not the intention of the opposition to put up with it very long. If they want the business of this House to be proceeded with, they must conduct themselves as the opposition always do and treat them respectfully. It was at the request of Sir Mackenzie Bowell that I had an interview with Sir Charles Tupper and brought these two gentlemen together. They made the arrangement that Sir Charles Tupper would conduct the session and then he would become the Prime Minister. That was the agreement that was made and these gentlemen had nothing to do with the arrangements, further until after the arrangement was fully concluded between Sir Mackenzie Bowell and Sir Charles Tupper.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Public buildings-Antigonish, $15,000.

This is a vote for the purpose of erecting a building in Antigonish to take the place of the building there which is very old. It has been there for a number of years [DOT] and it has been reported by the architect of the department to be in a very bad state of repair, so bad, in fact, that it would not be in the public interest to attempt to repair it. Therefore I am asking a vote of $15,000 towards the erection of a new building.
Before this goes through there are certain items of information we would like to have. In the first place what has been spent on that so far ?
No expenditure has yet been made.
What is this public building to include ?
This will house the postoffice and customs, and will also include a residence.
What building is there at present ?
The old building I spoke of, a frame building 50 feet by 32 feet, two and a half stories high.
Owned by the government?
Owned by the government.
Is that to be pulled down?
Yes. I think the intention in this case is to use the site on which the old building stands.
Are the plans made for this building?
The plans are in course of preparation and are nearly completed.
What is the estimate of the minister, formed on those plans, as to the cost?
The estimate for the building is about $25,000 complete.
Will the minister read the different items ? It is well to have these on ' Hansard,' so that in another year we can have them to refer to.

The estimates are : for the building itself, $16,000; heating, $2,000; electric wiring and fixtures, $600; fittings and furniture, including letter-boxes, $3,000 ; fencing and sidewalks, about $500; clerk of works, $1,000; and the usual sum for contingencies, making $25,000.
What is the population and the postal, customs and internal revenues of Antigonish?
The population is about 1,900, the postal revenue for 1903-4, $3,702, and the customs revenue, $7 7.80.
What do you pay the postmaster there?
With regard to that question the same duplicity arises from the Public Works Department acting practically as the agent for the other departments. That is information which I have not got.

We must have that kind of information. We have always had it previously. The ministers have been going along in a very slipshod way in the matter of supplying information for the committee. I want to serve a notice, a very kindly notice, on the ministers that they must not come here and attempt to put their estimates through on information which is altogether insufficient for the committee to accept. We are to be treated as a serious House who have the revenues of the country in their keeping to a certain extent, and it is not just because a minister puts a sum of money before us and says he is going io put up a building of stone or wood, that it must go through. We always had this Mr. FOSTER.
kind of information in my time, and if the minister hasu't it, he had better shut his book, and let some other minister who has the information that we require take the floor, and we will go on.

I think the hon. gentleman is asking rather too much. He has a perfect right to ask what the revenue of the post office is; but when he proceeded with the further question as to the salary of the postmaster, it seems to me that he went outside of what has been customary. It would lead to a discussion of how the Post Office Department is conducting its business, and whether it is paying postmasters more than it should, which are questions which cau only properly come up when the Post Office estimates are before the committee.

The hon. gentleman knows a great deal of what other people's ideas and motives are. He will allow me to state my own motive in asking this question. I had no such object as he has intimated. Here is a town of 1,900 people in which it is proposed to spend $25,000 in erecting a post office. We have a great many towns of 1,900 people which have no public building at all. and what I am trying to get at is what the revenues of this town are at present, and what the cost of the administration of this building will be after it is constructed. You are going to have a different kind of post office arrangement, I presume, after you get this building, and it will be more costly. What I am trying to get at is whether it is a wise proceeding to put up a $25,000 building which will afterwards have all these excesses of expenditure which the present building does not have. Another point I want to get at is whether there is any principle in this matter at all-whether every town which has 1,900 inhabitants and is fairly situated in comparison with Antigonish, is to have a public building. I remember that the opposition of former days, among them my hon. friend himself, went very actively into this question of the principle that underlay the policy of erecting public buildings, and protested most vehemently against erecting them in towns of a certain population when other towns of larger population were without them, saying that they were granted by favour and not on a broad public principle. They went so far as to propose a resolution, which was moved by Mr. David Mills, then a member of this House, in which they laid down certain principles that should guide. The names of these public buildings are legion, and we ought to arrive at some kind of policy or principle underlying these expenditures.

I do not want to intervene in the discussion; but the hon. member made a remark giving notice to all the ministers, and I thought I would draw at-

tention to the matter. I was not imputing any motives to him-quite the contrary. But when he asked a question as to the cost of the management of the post office, 1 pointed out that that was a subject on which the Minister of Public Works could not be expected to be informed; that would properly come up under the post office estimates. The hon. gentleman says he supposes the cost of collecting the revenue will be increased. I do not think that will be the case. I do not suppose it will be altered at all by the fact of the post office being in a building instead of in a rented building. It was to that one point that I directed my attention, not to the other questions of the hon. gentleman, which he had a perfect right to ask. The remuneration given to the postmaster for the services he renders does seem to me an unreasonable question to ask of the Minister of Public Works.

The hon. gentleman's point is that this is not relevant to the estimates. I would regard it as rather difficult to take that position, and I am sure that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works has over and over again answered questions which have been very much less relevant than that proposed by my hon. friend from North Toronto. We have got somewhat into the habit, during the past few years when the estimates are being discussed in committee, of accepting the stereotyped answer from the minister in charge that he is not in a position to give the information required as that comes under another department. That is one way of getting the estimates through, but perhaps it is not the best after all, and it should be the duty of ministers of the Crown to be present while the estimates are going through ; whether they happen to be in charge of the particular department whose estimates are being discussed or not, so that the House may get all .the information required.
Sir WILLIAM MULOCI-C. What is wanted ?

The salary of the postmaster. It is not at all an adequate answer for the Minister of Public Works to tell us that he is not able to furnish the information asked for. The minister of the department who can furnish the information ought to be here to give it.

The drift of my question is this. What is the position of the post office there now as regards salary and what changes, if any, will be made when the new building is finished and the post office moved into it ? Will the postmaster be put on a different footing and the expenditure increased ?

What population must a town have to entitle it to a public building ?
Sir WILLIAM MULOCIv. There has been no rule laid down by any government. I have no desire to provoke any discussion or to blame any government, but I can remember quite well when we in opposition took very serious exception to the erection of a public building at Lapraire.
And at Farnham You held up the House two days on Unit item.
The Laprairie post office, I think, had a revenue of $500.
