speechtext: Something like Antigouish.

No, Antigomsh has a revenue of nearly $4,000, and I think at Laprairie you put up a building that cost some $20,000. I think it is well to put up public buildings in places where they were required for public convenience. Of course it is one thing to have an idea, as my hon. friend says, and another thing to live up to it, but I think after all this item has a good deal more to commend it than some which , my hon. friends opposite sanctioned in the past.
Is the hon. gentleman now expressing contrition for his past V
I am afraid that remark is out of order. We have agreed, after our little discussion just now, to bury the hatchet for the present.
What will be the staff that will be housed there ?
There will be an office ic that building for the government engineers and for the Customs.
The information will be found in my report in the Appendix, letter ' C.' The items for Antigonish are as follows:	i
What customs officers are there there now ?
Only one.
One customs officer, one postmaster and no engineer at present.
There is a government engineer there now and also his assistant.
There are the chief engineer, his assistant, a clerk and a stenographer.
They are not for Anti-gonisli itself, but for a certain district ?
For the eastern district, of which Antigonish is the centre.
Have you an engineer in the post office now ?
I mean the engineer representing the Department of Public Works in that locality. [DOT]
You have an engineer and an assistant engineer ?

Yes.
Mr. I< OSTER. These have no connection with the building ?
No, but they will be housed there.
Is there any Inland Revenue office there ?
No.

When the hon. minister makes this expenditure of $25,000, which will carry $1,000 for interest besides the cost of a keeper with a pretty large salary to take care of that building and the cost of fuel and lighting and repairs and all that, he is making a pretty large inroad in our revenue. That $25,000 building will have in it, one postmaster, one or two clerks, one customs officer, and an engineer and his assistant. That seems a pretty large sum to invest in a building to house that number of the country's servants.

But it is not merely put up to house the officials. Antigonish has a population of 1,900, and the public will have free access to the post office and the other offices, so that they will utilize the building to a considerable extent.

Can the hon. gentleman give us an estimate of the amount of public money expended in this country on wharfs and breakwaters and for various other purposes in addition to this public building within the last eight or nine years?
Mr. HY'MAN. I am afriad if I had tried to prepare that class of information with regard to these votes, it would have taken some time. The question is not such as one would expect to be asked in putting through a vote of this kind, and therefore I am not prepared with the information.

So far as I am concerned I have all the information I want with respect to this vote. But, as we are considering votes for other public buildings, opportunities may arise for the minister to state what principle or policy he intends to follow hereafter in these matters.

Has the minister fixed $25,000 as the entire cost of this building and its fittings, or is this only an estimate which may be exceeded by ten or twenty thousand dollars ? I believe that in the erection of these public buildings, the minister, in the first place, should determine how much money he is ready to expend on a public building in the particular town for which it is intended. It seems to me that he proposes here to spend a pretty large sum for a town of only 1,800 population. However, we will let that go. What I desire to know is whether this amount is the outside limit. Has the minister instructed his architect, or whoever is to have supervision of this work or the making of the plans, that $25,000 must complete the building, with lighting and heating appliances and all its internal fittings ? If the minister has not done so, I think he ought to inform the House that this vote is simply a preliminary step. In bygone years, I have discussed this question. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Sutherland) for whom the present incumbent is acting temporarily, told us last year, or the year before, that he approved of that policy and that public buildings should be erected within the cost given. In other words, the minister told us that he would instruct those in charge of these works that in each case they must cut the coat according to the cloth furnished them-that no more cloth would be furnished to complete the garment. If the acting minister has not given that instruction to the officers, I hope he will be candid enough to tell us that we may know whether this $25,000 is to be the total amount expended on this work, or whether we may expect to be called upon to vote a very much larger sum. I shall feel it my duty to oppose with all my power the estimate for every public building unless that principle is applied. Unless that principle is applied, we cannot tell in what expenditure we are involving the country. Some years ago I advocated this principle very strongly.
I also advocated the principle that in small towns the size of Antigonish. public buildings should be erected for a smaller sum than is here proposed. I think that a building sufficient to meet the wants of a town of this size might be provided for a very much smaller sum. When we think of the enormous number of incorporated towns and villages in this country that have not had a dollar of public money expended within their borders-and at the rate at which we are going will not for fifty years to come have a public building of any kind-the condition is alarming. Unfortunately, in the county I have the honour to represent,

we have not a town as large as Antigonish -possibly 1,600 or 1,700 Is the largest town we have, and we have five of about the same size. To all appearances it will be many a long day before that county will have the opportunity of having money expended on public buildings within its borders, though, I am sure that it is just as important a county as Antigonish. 1 would be glad if the minister would take all these matters into consideration, and would not be guided simply by some special reasdn for giving one town a public building and, because that reason did not apply, refusing it to another town. Now, in the case of Clinton, I have it on the authority of the late member for West Huron that when he spoke to the architect of the Public Works 1 lepartment with reference to the estimate for a post office in that town-a post officei which the former Minister of Public Works, Hon. Mr. Tarte said, was to be erected as a model post office at a cheap rate, to include a postmaster's residence and so do away with the necessity for any caretaker besides the postmaster-the officer of the department said that the policy of the department was not to make plans and specifications . for a building costing less than $10,000. I would like to know who runs this government and this country. It does not seem to be even the ministers. The country seems to be run and the expenditure fixed by the departmental officers. I do not think it lies in the mouth of any officer of the government to say that he will not make plans and specifications for a building costing less than a certain sum, even though parliament may consider that sum all that is necessary. If that is the rule of the department, I am sorry that the minister has not better control of the affairs committed to his charge. If I were Minister of Public Works-which I never expect to be-I would quickly tell that officer that I had no further use for his services, and that I would put in a man who could make plans and specifications for a building costing whatever sum I thought necessary to spend upon it. Of course, we must hold the minister responsible for the conduct of his officers. As I have said, if the departmental officers will not conform to the requirements of the ministers, it will be a very difficult matter indeed for this House to control the public expenditure. I do not know who the officer was who made the statement to which I have referred, but I think the time has gone by, if it ever existed, when officers of the department should dictate to this House or to the minister what the cost of public buildings should be. The minister should lay down as a principle that the estimate for a public building must be adhered to. And we must hold the minister absolutely responsible for carrying out the construction of public buildings within the estimate, or we
can exercise no control over public expenditure.

I am sure there must have been some misunderstanding as between the late member for West Huron and the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson), if the impression was conveyed that officers of the department would not draw plans for any building for which the minister had given orders. It may be, in the case which was under discussion, that the chief official of the department who has control of the erection of buildings, thought that it would have been impossible to construct a building for the services which it was proposed to make it for, at a less sum than $10,000. In the case to which the hon. gentleman refers, the town of Clinton, the actual construction of the building cost $9,650. So far as the estimate of the building is concerned, I want to say this, which is general in its character, that when this House has given its fiat by a majority that a public building shall be constructed in a certain place, it behooves us to put up a building of such a character that it will be a credit to the place in which it is erected. It is well understood that public buildings cannot be built of the same character as many others. Possibly, the officers of the department may err occasionally in making a building too heavy, possibly they are putting too much money into it. But, speaking with the responsibility of acting Minister of Public Works, I may say that I think that is a good fault, in the long run it saves an expenditure upon the buildings in the way of future repairs. I- think, taking everything into consideration, it is in the best interest of the country that when we erect a public building it should be of a character which will do credit to the government So far as the estimates are concerned, I have taken great care in having them properly prepared. I was assured by the officers of the department that a building such as is requisite here can be erected for the sum of $16,000. I have already given to the House, and it is on the ' Hansard,' the estimates of the officer for that building. Now, it is to be remembered that the cost of a building of that character, for a custom-house and post office, with the cost of furnishing the building separately, may be much larger than the cost of any other building in the locality where it is erected. I acknowledge that when this House is voting money they are entitled to all that information, and, so far as I am concerned, I hope to be able to keep the expenditure within the estimate. There may be circumstances in a large public building which may require the expenditure to exceed the estimate, but I can assure the House that special care will be taken to keep the expenditure within the estimates which are voted by the House.
When was this Antigonish building decided upon ?

The question of erecting that building lias been pressed upon tbe attention of the department for some time. For two or three years there was a question as to whether it would be better to repair it or to build a new building. The last reports we have say that the sills are so rotten that portions of them can be pulled away by hand. The building has been getting jnto a bad shape. The government own both the site and the building.
Of what material is tbe new building ?
It is to be a brick structure on a stone foundation.

Now that the government own the site, I think this proposition is still more unjustifiable. A more ridiculous expenditure, it seems to me, could scarcely be conceived of. We are not here merely to build a monument to the respected gentleman who has the honour to represent Antigonish. Here is Antigonish, not even an incorporated town.
Oh, yes it is.

Then the census lies. It gives the population at 1,888 souls, and we are taking $25,000, in addition to owning the land, to build a custom-house, which, I understand, is also to be used as a post office. We had better put $10,000 into the building, and get accommodation outside for the engineer and his assistants. As the hon. member for Hafton (Mr. Henderson) has said, we have hundreds of towns needing accommodation more than this one. I have two or three in my own county, and I do not ask for one-half the amount the government is expending in the county of Antigonish. There is the town of St. Andrews, a very important watering place on the Atlantic sea-board, with a population very nearly equal to that of Antigonish, with a very large revenue indeed ; and it has a post office and custom-house in a small wooden building that certainly is no credit to the government. Then there is the town of Milltown, with a population of 2, 044. If the Postmaster General would come down there he would be ashamed of the public building in that town. I think this amount should be divided in two, and half of it be given to some other place, if it is desired to do justice. I have in my hand a little circular, I am not sure it was not got up with the complicity of the acting Minister of Public Works. It says ' Vote for a new building for St. George : vote for Mr. Gilmour.' St. George is in my county. I do not see anything in the estimates for that St. George building ; but I trust the minister will see his way to carry out the suggestion made in that circular when the supplementary estimates are brought down.

In many towns with a smaller population than that of Antigonish, Mr. FOSTER.
in various parts of Canada, public buildings have been provided ; at the same time, I am free to admit that many towns with a larger population than Antigonish have not yet been provided with public buildings. But it is a fact that has been recognized by both political parties that Antigonish, according to its population, is a much more important town than many others in Nova Scotia or elsewhere with a greater population. It is the shire town of the county of Antigonish, and has a university, the only university in eastern Nova Scotia. The importance of Antigonish has been recognized, not only by this government, but recognized by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in power. Away back, some twenty-five years or more, when the policy of erecting public buildings was being inaugurated, Antigonish was recognized as a place where the government should erect a public building. The only difference, therefore, between the two parties in regard to Antigonish is that the Conservative party went about putting up a public building in the wrong way, and the Liberal party has gone about it in the right way. In 1882 the late Conservative government purchased in the town of Antigonish, for the purpose of a public building, an old wooden building used as the St. Francois Xavier College. The authorities of the college undertook to build a brick building in a different part of the town and sold the old buildirig to the then government. I am not finding fault with that at all, except with the way in which it was done. They sold to the government of the day the old building with the lot, for a very moderate sum indeed- But I say the late government went about it the wrong way. They should have done what the present government is doing-built upon that lot a new building of brick suitable for the requirements of the town at that time. But what did they do ? They bought the building and the lot, and undertook to repair the old building, and year after year appropriations were placed in the estimates by the late government for purposes of repair, tearing down the walls and building them up again, tearing out the rotten sills, and the roof, and remodelling it, so that it has cost nearly as much, at least half as much, as it would have cost to put up a new building. What is the result ?
Notwithstanding all the expenditures that were made year after year and the interest charges accumulating, the result has been that, through age, its condition and wear and tear it became absolutely unsuited to the needs of the post office or of the officers who are occupying the building. I brought the matter to the attention of the government for several years and they refused to do anything. At last they were compelled to send an officer from the Department of Public Works to examine the building, a thorough examination was made of it and it was condemned; so that it be-

came absolutely necessary to erect a new building in Antigonish. As to the cost, as to the dimensions and as to the kind of building that should be put up in Antigonish I desire to say a few words. This is a very important point. Nobody who knows the conditions which prevail there can deny that. It is important that we should have a large building because the resident engineers for the eastern section of the province of Nova Scotia have been located in Antigonish for the last thirty years. The province is divided into two districts as far as public works are concerned. The engineers of the western part are located in Halifax while those of the eastern part have their residences and offices at Antigonish. Therefore this is not used as an ordinary public building for the accommodation of the postmaster and his staff, and the collector of customs and his staff, but a building must be provided to suit the growing requirements of the resident engineers and their assistants not only for the county of Antigonish but for the eastern part of the province of Nova Scotia. The sum which it is estimated this building will cost is not at all a large one. It will be a very respectable building indeed and will afford ample accommodation to these various public officers to which I have referred. The cost of maintenance will not be any more than it was before. We have had to keep a janitor for the last twenty-two years in charge of the old building which, on account of its age, is a very much more difficult building to take care of and keep in proper condition than an up to date modern building will be. I think the estimate for the new building is not a large one. The building will be a very modest one for the requirements of the town.

I think it w'ould be very difficult for any one to get a justification out of that speech. I would like to know if the hon. gentleman had anything to do with the distribution of this circular :
Vote for a new public building in Antigonish.

No, I never deemed it necessary to refer, even in my elections, to any appropriations made for public buildings or any other work. It was so difficult for the Conservative party to get a man to run against me in the county that they had to import a man from another county for appearance sake.
Well then, you do not need a building.
No. I do not need a building or a public -work of any kind to get votes. But, the town of Antigonish needs it and it is only right that they should gel a fair share of the good things that are going.

Being a new member I am not very familiar with these estimates.
but in looking over the appropriations for Manitoba, a country in which the conditions are changing very much more rapidly than they are in the east, I find that outside of the amounts put down for the constituency of the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) who represents the riding north of mine and outside of the city of Winnipeg, his right arm, there is only $15,000 in the estimates for public buildings for that great province which is developing so rapidly. I am surprised that any business government-
You need not he surprised. -

Perhaps it is because I am a new member-but I am surprised that $25,000 should be placed in the main estimates for a public building in Antigonish, a town of 1.800 inhabitants. I think the population has been 1,800 for some time, it will likely be 1.800 for the next twenty-five years, and it is not likely that they will want any additional buildings. I believe this is not a fair estimate for a building in a town of that size in the eastern country. In estimating the probable requirements of a town in the next twenty years with the view of erecting a public building there is no possible comparison to be made between the east and the west. The development of the west is going ahead so rapidly that such comparison is impossible. AVhile a town in the west may to-day have only 1,800 inhabitants the prospects are that in ten years the population will be ten times as great. And we should therefore prepare for the future, but there can be no justification offered for erecting a building in the expectation of an equally rapid development in old Nova Scotia.

I presume the hon. gentleman (Mr. Schaffner) who has just taken his seat knows that these estimates are not the estimates in which new expenditures are initiated. These are the main estimates. These are revotes and consequently it is impossible to say what may appear in the estimates for the province which the hon. gentleman represents.
Well then they do not mean anything.

Alay I ask the hon. Alinister of Public Works if it is the intention of the department to provide for the erection of a post office in the town of Seafortb. The post office revenue exceeds the post office revenue of the town of Wingham in the constituency of my hon. friend from East Huron (Mr. Chisholm) yet a new post office was erected in Wingham at a very large cost-$15,000 or $20,000. I am not finding any fault with the expenditure of that money because I believe it was necessary, but I would like to know if the hon. minister has in contemplation the erection of

a post office in our town. I have just arisen to endeavour to obtain this information because many of my constituents are interested in knowing whether the hon. minister intends to erect such a building. I may say for the information ,of the hon. minister that the post office at present in use in our town is a very old building indeed. It has been in existence for more than a third of a century and a new one has become a public necessity. Complaints are frequent in our town that the present building does not.afford the necessary facilities for handling the business there. I am sure that if the hon. minister understood the necessities of the town of Seaforth he would at once conclude to erect a building in that town worthy of the position which it holds in the county. As far as the policy of erecting public buildings is concerned, I see by the estimates that a post office is to be erected in the village of Antigonish in tiie province of Nova Scotia at a cost of $25,000. It is not my intention to ask the hon. minister to erect a building, costing anything like that sum of money, nor do I believe the people of my constituency desire it. We will be- very well satisfied with an expenditure of, say, $10,000. We have a population in the neighbourhood of 2,600, and I am perfectly confident that if the hon. minister would see to it that an amount of $10,000 was included in the estimates our people would be very well pleased and the probabilities are that when the next general election comes around they would not return a Conservative representative, but would send a follower of the government.

I shall be very glad indeed to take into consideration any representations which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gunn) may make as to the necessity of a public building in the town of Seaforth. .Speaking from memory I do not think that the county of Huron has done so badly in the way of public buildings.
It is a large county.
Quite true, but there are other large counties. There is a public building at Goderich, another at Clinton and another at Wingham.
But. the hon. minister-
May I be permitted to say a word once in a while without being interrupted?
I will not interrupt the hon. minister if he is so fastidious.

I am not fastidious at all. On almost every occasion on which I rise to speak I am interrupted. Surely the hon. gentleman can allow the county of Anti gonish a public building. There are three in Huron and if the hon. gentleman has any representations to make in regard to a public Mr. GUNN.
building at Seaforth I shall be glad to listen to those representations.
I was going to remark to the minister, who is very fastidious-he is not always so fastidious-and 11 he was not so fastidious we might make better progress
Mr. Chairman

I was going to sug gest to him that in enumerating the public works carried out in Huron he omitted to mention some harbour improvements in Goderich. That is a very convenient omission. I would take the opportunity of pointing out that Seaforth has an income from the post office of $1,000 more than Antigonish and the minister might properly see his way to spending $1,000.
I would like to put on record the customs revenue of, Antigonish. The receipts were $1,024.03. You can add that to the post office receipts and you have the grand total.
Did I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the customs receipts are only $1,000 ?
That is the amount given at page 745 of the Auditor General's Report. If this report is not correct he can settle that with the minister.

The minister was in Brantford during the recent election campaign and viewed our post office at that time. It cost about $25,000 according to competent experts. We have a population of about 19,000 and we have received no additions to the post office since its erection. It houses the Post Office Department, the Customs Department and the Inland Revenue Department, which together produce a revenue of about $350,000 per annum. We have had no expenditure there on public buildings for a great many years. While we are wandering rather far afield I shall briefly discuss with my hon. friend the question which he has raised. I did visit Brantford, I did see the public building of Brantford. I would not like to say that it is such a building as I would like to see the Department of Public Works erect in Brantford. There have been some expenditures made on that building. I interviewed, I think, the proper parties there, that is the custom house officer and the postmaster, and they assured me that if these expenditures were made upon the building it would vastly improve the service they were able to render. The hon. gentleman forgot to tell the House that the Department of Public Works are making a large expenditure in Brantford. He says they are practically making no expenditure there. 1 was pleased to see the drill hall there, I think it is a credit to the city of Brantford. There is an expenditure on that building and in these very estimates we are asking a vote for a continuation of this work. I think if the hon. member (Mr. Cockshutt) wants to be fair he should thank the Department of Public Works in reference to that public building. A building has been erected there but I do not suppose the Postmaster General is responsible for the size ol' the building. I am not aware either how much it cost definitely but I was informed last summer when visiting Sarnia that it cost $70,000 to $80,000. What I complain of is that I cannot for the life of me see where $70,000 or $80,000 is put in that building.
For an expenditure of $70,000 or $80,000 we ought certainly to have a building of large capacity. The town of Sarnia is a growing town, a town which will probably double its population within the next ten years, and its requirements will far exceed

those of the present time. During the last summer when I was in Sarnia I went into the post office, and I was astonished to find that the portion of the building alloted to the public was, to my mind, entirely too cramped and narrow and quite unsuited to the needs of a town of a population of 8,000 or 9,000. I was anxious to see where the officers did the sorting, and after being allowed to look in, I was astonished to find that it was equally cramped. The whole building was entirely too shallow. As a matter of curiosity I asked what kind of an office the postmaster had, and I succeeded in haying a look into a little box of about eight feet square. I said: ' When I see the Postmaster General I am going to tell him that he ought to be ashamed of himself to put a public postmaster into such a cramped space.' The result in this case is not what I would expect from an expenditure of so large a sum of money.

I do not know how the building is laid out. I suppose my officers were consulted. I was in Halifax some time ago and went into the postmaster's office there. I do not know who erected that building, we or our predecessors, but the postmaster's room was no bigger than an ordinary box stall; I do not think it was more than six feet square. However, 1 suppose the real point of my hon. friend's remarks is that we have not a large enough building at Sarnia. His complaint is practically that we are too economical. So that it is hard to please him.

The building was constructed in the usual way, by public contract. I have never before heard the first breath of complaint against the building. I have always understood that the people of Sarnia are pleased with it and consider it a credit to the town. I ask because we remember that last year an hon. gentleman who, I regret, is not in the House at the present time, and who was very conversant with the shipping interests of this country. especially the shipping of perishable products, made a very serious complaint on the floor of this House, against the character of the 'equipment for the purpose of carrying perishable goods from Canada to the old land. I think it was with reference to the very statement made by the hon. gentleman that has been alluded to, and who was a member of the House at that time. The Allans were communicated with, and perhaps I had better read the answer that he received to his communication calling their attention to what had been said. It was addressed to Mr. O'Hara, of the Department of Trade and Commerce :
Montreal, October 4, 1904.
F. C. T. O'Hara, Esq.,
Department of Trade and Commerce,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-We duly received your various communications in this matter. We have also ' 28
read carefully the printed sheets containing the debates in the House of Commons on this subject, and more particularly the statements made by Mr. Smith, M.P.
When we entered into contracts with the government to furnish refrigerator stowage, the temperature most suitable for butter was thought to be about 30 degrees of Fahr. and this temperature was provided. Within a short time, however, after the system was in operation butter exporters commenced an agitation for 10 degrees lower temperature. After considerable demur we met this demand by altering all former arrangements, giving additional power and a larger service of freezing pipes.
These alterations involved an outlay of $23,910.72 as by the specifications and vouchers now before the department, one moiety of which is reasonably due us by the government.
There is now provided on the vessels of our Montreal service refrigerator facilities for the better conveyance of perishable cargo as follows (1) compartments for frozen goods at a temperature- varying from 20 to 30 degrees; (2) compartments for cheese, bacon, fruits, &e., with a temperature of from 35 to 40 degrees, higher or lower as may be wanted by the shippers of the goods, and (3) compartments with forced currents of external air (inlets and outlets) operated by steam-driven fans.
Details of these various facilities are explained more fully in our recent circulars to shippers, copies of which we inclose for your information. Still more detailed information is given in the typewritten memorandum sent herewith prepared by our Glasgow friends and bearing the date of March 22, 1904.
As stated above, the arrangement to give a temperature below 30 degrees was on the- demand of butter shippers. Few of these merchants, however, furnished their goods to the ship at any such degree of cold. We inclose official statements given to us by ..the Montreal government officers having the matter in charge, from which you will note that out of 31 separate shipments made in July of the current year, only six were delivered to the ship at or below 32 degrees, that six were delivered at and above 52 degrees and that the average temperature of the whole 31 shipments was above 41 degrees. We have more than once suggested that a rule should be promulgated by the department requiring that all shipments should be delivered to the ocean ship at or below the temperature which is to be maintained in the compartment wherein they are stowed throughout the voyage.
The machinery of these compartments is arranged to maintain the required temperature, but is not calculated to reduce the temperature of butter delivered at or above 52 degrees down to the minimum. Such reductions should be made in city refrigerators prior to delivery being given to the ship.
As regards deliveries of refrigerator goods to consignees at British ports, we have (broadly speaking) to complain that consignees are extremely dilatory in receiving their goods: not infrequently they are left on the wharfs for a full day after they have been discharged, and occasionally even two days. We receive occasional statements from our British friends giving details of these delays which we communicate to the shippers.
Respecting the returns made to the department of the temperatures registered by the thermographs, it should be borne1 in mind that we not infrequently make an agreement with



the shipper fixing the temperature which is to be maintained throughout the voyage in the compartment containing his goods. It may thus occur that while the thermograph registers 40 degrees in a compartment containing butter, our agreement with the shipper nfay nevertheless have been carried out. We have explained this matter to your Montreal agents who called our attention to the circumstances that butter was being carried at a higher temperature than our contract with the government required.
We return the papers sent us by you whereon we have penciled the information asked for.
Any further information you may require in the premises will be cheerfully furnished.
Yours truly,
(Signed) H. & A. ALLAN.

The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) will observe that it was owing to the comments that were made last session by the late member for South Wentworth (Mr. Smith) that this letter is written, and these are the explanations they give. It would appear from this that improvements have been made at additional cost to themselves. But they point out that the steamers cannot be held alone responsible, that the shippers themselves are partly to blame, as they deliver goods at a higher temperature than they should.
Did the government pay half of that increased cost ?
No, it was not entertained ; they had to pay it themselves.

I am rather pleased at the statement made by the minister, so far as it goes. It seems to meet the case very well. However, in my recollection, [DOT]one of the serious complaints made by the late member for South Wentworth, and which we are very glad has been taken notice of by the shippers, was that these agreements or conditions were not carried out during the entire voyage across the ocean ; that whilst butter was put on hoard ship at a certain temperature, which was maintained for a day or so, this temperature was not kept up during the entire voyage, and the result was disastrous to the shipper. Now, to my mind, the Department of Trade and Commerce should give special attention to that point, and see that all the requirements which entitle them to this subsidy and all the promises made are carried out through the entire voyage, so that butter, for example, will not be put on board ship at a temperature of say 30 degrees and be brought down during the first day or two to a temperature of 20,/ but that that temperature should be maintained during the entire voyage, instead of allowing it to run up probably to 30 or 40 again, to the injury of the goods. I am glad attention has been drawn to the fact that when goods are landed on the other side consignees have been neglectful in looking Mr. PATERSON.
after those goods. I scarcely see that the department could be held responsible for that, providing due notice is given of the arrival of those goods. It is certainly, to my mind, the duty of the consignee at once to take the goods away, and not allow an article such as butter to remain upon the dock at Liverpool for possibly ten or eleven days. I tbink, in some circumstances, goods were allowed to remain that length of time, of course to the great injury of the article, and to the detriment of the entire Canadian industry. I hope the department will take steps to see that these conditions are complied with throughout the entire voyage, and that we will not have a renewal of the complaints that were made last year-that that feature of the contract was overlooked, I would ask the Minister of Agriculture if he is still of opinion that 20 degrees of cold is sufficient for the transhipment of butter? I understood last year he had arrived at the conclusion that it was necessary to bring it down to 10 degrees. It seems that the provision here made is for 20.

From the investigations I have made, I am of the opinion that 2Q/ degrees is a cold enough temperature in which to carry butter from Canada to England in a steamship. The butter is put upon the market as soon as it gets to England, and there is no particular reason in having it below 20 degrees.

There seems to be one other matter that requires the careful attention of the department, and that is that ample provision should be made for fjbrwarding these perishable products to the place of shipment. I do not know what arrangement has been made with the railway companies, but it would certainly seem very essential that some method of refrigeration be provided, so that the goods will arrive at the port of shipment at the degree of temperature at which the shipowners, Messrs. Allan, have referred. If butter or other delicate articles are presented to them for shipment at a temperature which will be almost destructive, we can hardly expect that they can provide means by which their quality or utility will be restored. I am not aware whether the hon. minister has any system of providing refrigerator ears for the purpose of forwarding goods, such as have been referred to, to the point of shipment.	,
In reply to the hon. gentleman, I would say that we have, but perhaps it would be better when my estimates come up to go into the details of that question.

There is another thing disclosed by this correspondence, which, it seems to me, is worth while referring to. That is the complaint that there were no thermographs in the various chambers. There is nothing said about them in the

correspondence, listening casually, as I did, to it being read. The question was asked if all necessary provision had been made in that direction and strenuous complaint was made by my hon. friend from Wentworth (Mr. Smith), that there were only a certain number of thermographs provided for each vessel, that they were placed in some of the chambers but not in others, and that there were no means of registering the temperature from day to day in these chambers. Then, the correspondence discloses this further fact that the Messrs. Allan claim that they have fulfilled their agreement in regard to the temperature at which they were to keep the chambers for butter. They were to keep the chambers at thirty degrees but they point out that the government, after making the contract, found out that ten degrees lower would be a better temperature for butter, and the hon. minister told us last year that down as low as eleven degrees would be a better temperature. If that be the fact then the government are to blame because their expert must have known before the contract was entered into which was the most suitable temperature. It turns out that thirty degrees is not the best temperature by any means, and while there is a difference between the hon. minister and those who complain regarding these arrangements the two facts which are brought out by that letter are that the Allans have fulfilled their contract and that the fault was with the hon. Minister of Agriculture in entering into the contract without providing for a proper temperature but in providing for a temperature about ten degrees above what it ought to have been.

I may explain that there were two sets of contracts, one made by the Department of Trade and Commerce for vessels which are subsidized by ft he department and which vessels by these contracts now are required to provide adequate cold Storage. There was another set of contracts entered into by my department some years ago with vessels that were subsidized and some not subsidized by the government under the ordinary class of subsidy. But I entered into contracts as the Minister of Agriculture to induce them to equip themselves with cold storage. These contracts lasted for three years. At the end of these contracts these vessels were free of any control by the government. The subsidy contracts made by the Department of Trade and Commerce have been continuous and the vessels operating under these contracts are still controlled to a certain extent by the government. My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) has spoken about temperatures. I do not know that at the present time it is worth while going into that question but I would point out that a temperature of thirty degrees which was provided for when we first made the contracts for cold storage was the temperature which at that time the dealers in butter wanted, expected and asked for the carriage of their butter. As time went on it developed that butter could be more securely carried at a lower temperature and from time to time we urged upon the steamship companies to make their temperature lower, which they did. as far as they could, with the equipment they then had. Our contracts censed. We had no control over them. They, however, in view of tile demand made, lowered their temperature for butter. They have in most of these steamers two or three different compartments. In a great many yessels they have one compartment for the carriage of butter or other articles which can be

frozen. The temperature of that compartment is brought down to about twenty'and sometimes a little below. They have another compartment for products that, while they want to be carried cold, cannot bear to t>e frozen-cheese and fruit, for instance and many meats which the people do not wish to have frozen but want to have chilled. The temperature of these compartments has been maintained at from 32 to 36 degrees. Then, they have another set of compartments which are described in the Messrs. Allan's letters. Those are compartments through which chilled air is forced. The temperature in these compartments is not required to be as low as that of the compartment to which I last alluded. X forget for the moment wliat the exact temperature is but I think it is expected to be below 45, speaking, subject to correction, from memory. In any discussion of the temperature in a compartment it is absolutely necessary to know what the contents of that compartment are before you judge the temperature. I do not wish particularly to enter into a discussion but a statement has been made in regard to what was said by the hon. member for Wentworth last session. So far as the Allan line of steamers is concerned, I think hon, gentlemen are satisfied with that. I have some details I could give.

The trouble seems to be that the discussion has gone on to a certain extent, in which the Minister of Agriculture has reflected pretty severely on an absent member. That is now in 'Hansard' and is going into the papers, and it seems 'to be unfair for the other side of the case not to have tlie whole matter discussed at the present time, so that all will go on ' Hansard ' and to the public together, as it ought to. I ithink my hon. friend will have to take the disadvantages as well as the advantages of colleagues. Sometimes they are a great help, but sometimes they are a sad hindrance.

In all seriousness my hon. friend will see that if what he proposes now is adopted, it will take the committee away altogether from the subject under consideration to discuss an item which must come under investigation on another day.

But my hon. friend will see that there is butter as well as salt sea Mr. SAM. HUGHES.
in connection with this estimate, because the subsidy carries two things. The vessels have to sail the vast deep, and they have to carry butter and other things in a certain condition, and both are parts of the same contract.

Quite so, but I think it is not contended that the vessels for which I am asking this vote are not up to the requirements. If that be the case, that disposes of this vote and we had better get on, and the Minister of Agriculture and the ([DOT]tiler gentlemen can discuss the other matter at the proper time.
Mr. SPItOULE. 1 understand that we were to have cold storage for carrying perishable products. Are the vessels to provide cold storage or not ?	*
Certainly.

Then it is absolutely necessary for us to know what kind of cold storage they are going to provide, and whether the government have made a proper contract. The Minister of Agriculture contends that they have done that. We contend that he has contradicted the statements made by (Mr. Smith on the basis of the minister's own reports and on the thermographic readings of minimum and maximum temperature given in this House. We believe that Mr. Smith's statements were based on reliable and authentic information. These statements are contradicted by the minister now. Consequently we ought to have it settled whether Mr. Smith or the Minister of Agriculture is right.

I think the whole matter arose from a remark I made. When attention was called to Mr. Smith's statements, the deputy had just informed me that there were facts taken by Mr. Smith from vessels that were not subsidized by the government, and therefore the government could not be held responsible for them. That remark led to this discussion. But now we are discussing the Allan Line steamers, and perhaps I may as well read the provision for cold storage in the ' Bavarian.'
1 he compartment No. 5 low-er between decks has been divided by a bulkhead on the centre line of the ship, and the starboard chamber thus formed has been subdivided by a bulkhead athwartships. The space forward of the hatch to the water-tight bulkhead, of a capacity of 5,41S cubic feet, should be capable of being maintained at a minimum temperature of about twenty degrees, while the remainder of the space on the starboard side of a capacity 3,211 cubic feet, together with the whole of the compartment on the port side, of a capacity of 8,958 cubic feet, should be able to be maintained at a minimum temperature of about thirty-two degrees as above. In addition to the above,* there is also the compartment ip the centre of No. 5 main between decks, of a capacity of 4,780 cubic feet, capable of being maintained at a minimum temperature of about thirty-two degrees as beforp. The arrangement

of piping is such that each of the chambers can be maintained independently of the others, or cut off altogether if required. Total capacity, 22,367 cubic feet.
I have also the particulars with reference to the ' Corinthian,-' the ' Hungarian,' the Ionian,' the 'Numidian,' the 'Ontarian,' the ' Pomeranian,' the ' Pretorian,' the ' Sardinian,' the ' Sicilian' and the ' Tunisian.' So that the hon. gentleman will see that it is all right so far as this vote is concerned.

Oh, no, it is all wrong; that is the trouble. We have no information, or comparatively none. The hon. minister reads what should he on one vessel ; but does not tell us how much space or what temperature is provided for on the various boats. According to the minister's own statement some products require to be carried at a temperature of 11 degrees, yet the lowest provided is 20. We have not got the contract or any information as to what it contains, which was made with these steamship companies. All that the minister gives us is the spaces contained in one steamship.
Mr, PATERSON. I only gave that as a sample. I said nothing about 11. degrees.

But I did ; and that is just where I say the hon. minister shows they have not made pro'per provision. The Minister of Agriculture has told us that butter could be kept better in a temperature of 11 degrees than in a temperature of 20 or 30, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce told us that in some of these compartments the temperature is kept down to 30 degrees and in others to about 20. Does the contract bind the company to keep the compartments at any temperature ; and if so, what is the temperature, and how much space are they to provide with one temperature and how much with another ? What' provision is made for the thermographs ? How many of them are there, and are they self-registered ? Will there be one in each chamber ? Where it is possible a register should be kept of the temperature of every day in the voyage, and where the proper temperature is known which perishable fruits and other commodities require, surely it is the duty of the government to provide in their contract for that temperature during every day of the voyage, and for a thermographic registration every day in each compartment. If that were done, and these charts taken out, we could tell whether the temperature is proper or not, and whether the government has made proper provision to carry the farmers' produce as it should be in order to have it on the market in proper condition.
I find that the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. E. D. Smith) made observations on the 29th July other than those to which the hon. Minister of Agriculture refei'red.

I could not say positively without looking up ' Hansard.' * Mr. Smith spoke more than once on this question, but the particular occasion referred to by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) was that on which he took the thermographic records and quoted them. Afterwards I was able to take the same thermographic records and compare them with those quoted by Mr. Smith, and I found that he made this mistake, that he did not take into account the fact that in many of the vessels there was more than one thermographic record.
My hon. friend should quote Mr. Smith's statement.
I cannot do so just at the moment, but I am speaking in general terms.

It would be better for the hon. gentleman to defer any observation until he has the records with him.
1 find that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) rose and answered Mr. Smith on that occasion, and I do not find that any application was made to delay the reply of the government until the advent of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture, although he seems to think it was a most unfortunate circumstance that the defence of the government should have been entrusted to Sir Richard Cartwright rather than to himself. However that may be, I do find that the hon. gentleman was in his place answering questions on the 1st August, and had from that time until the end of the session to make, in the presence of Mr. Smith, the observations he has seen fit to make in his absence. It would have been far better if the hon. minister had not waited until Mr. Smith is not here to make what were undoubtedly intended as very serious reflections upon him.
I would not have alluded to the matter in any way whatever if Mr. Smith's observations had not been quoted to-night.

The hon. gentleman could have referred to them in a different spirit and tone and without making reflections on Mr. Smith, and could thus have justified the decision of the government equally as well. There was a little too much spite in his remarks.

Mr. Smith obtained the thermographic records from the Minister of Agriculture by asking questions across the floor. From these reports I read his statement. If there is anything -wrong in the statement Mr. Smith made which is the subject of criticism, it is because the minister furnished him with incorrect information. I hold that Mr. Smith was perfectly justified in using the information he obtained from the report of the Minister of

Agriculture and the questions answered across the floor. I cannot conceive for a moment that Mr. Smith presumed to give information to this House which he had not obtained from that authentic source. I say this in justification of an old friend who is not with us at this time. I regard the speech made by Mr. Smith then as one of the most important speeches delivered during the whole parliament. It showed a breadth of knowledge in the matter of transportation of perishable products which I believe was not possessed by any member in this House. I listened to the speech very carefully and have read and re-read many parts of it. and the one thing I felt I could rely upon was the correctness of the statement made by Mr. Smith, knowing the source from which he obtained his information.
I shall defer making any more remarks until my own estimates come up.

Where the lion. Minister of Agriculture did the hon. member for Wentworth an injustice was in making the charge that Mr. Smith had reference to the ventilation of defective apples and not defective butter and cheese. That statement cannot be borne out by the record, because on page 794 of last year's ' Hansard ' you will see that Mr. Smith asked the Minister of Agriculture whether the government irf-spector had examined the compartments in certain vessels, and what system of mechanical ventilation was in each. Again, on July 11th, 1904, he asked about mechanical ventilation on steamers, and the hon. gentleman answered the question. Again, on April ISth, he put this question :
1.	In answer to question of April 6th, the Minister of Agriculture said
The steamship * Lake Champlain ' had the ordinary system of Cowl ventilation.
2.	Has the government examined these Cowl ventilators and found them in proper order and of sufficient size on this boat on each outward voyage when perishable cargo was on board ?
To these questions the hon. minister replied :
One of the inspectors for the Department of Agriculture has reported on each outward voyage of this steamship, both from the port of Montreal, both during the past season of navigation, and from the port of St. Johns, N.B., during the winter season, and in each report the ventilation is described as follows.
Then he went on to give the very statement quoted by Mr. Smith in this House. Yet, he now says that Mr. Smith's statements are incorrect. Mr. Smith, however, quoted the very information he got from the minister himself, and the minister is not justified in complaining about the conduct ' of Mr. Smith, because every one knows that there was no hon. gentleman in this House more conversant with the question than the hon. member for Wentworth, and I do not even exclude the hon. minister himself.
Are these steamers supplied with wireless telegraphy ?
The turbines are, and so are some of the others.
We require more information than has been given. We want to know something about the contract, so that we may satisfy ourselves
It is precisely the same contract.

But we were told that the contract was right in every respect. May we not be allowed to exercise our own judgment as to whether it was right or not? Why should we not be allowed to know what it actually provided for? Though we were assured that it was perfect it turned out to be very loosely drawn.

There was an observation in the report of Messrs. Allan respecting the condition in which goods were placed on board these ships. An hon. gentleman on this side has referred to the fact that a staff of inspectors is kept by the department of Agriculture at Montreal. I observe that that very circumstance is adverted to by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) in his speech of last year in reply to the member for Wentworth. Mr. Smith. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said:-
As regards what the Department of Agriculture has done, the department has furnished me with this memorandum. They state that the department maintains a staff of inspectors at Montreal to observe and report concerning the condition of Canadian food products when loaded in the steamers, including the shipments carried in cold storage..
Well, it seems a rather extraordinary condition of things, if the government have a staff of inspectors in Montreal, that they should be unaware that these goods were put in the cold storage apartments at too high a temperature. How does it happen that the attention of the government was not called to this fact by the government inspectors ?

A good deal of the information has been in the hands of the government. The fact, that goods, especially butter, arrive in Montreal at a higher temperature than they ought to have when put in the cold storage chambers in the ships is true, unfortunately. We have had our inspectors carefully watching that trade, and they have made reports. I have drawn the attention of the people who handle this butter to the difficulty, aud have explained to them the wrong they were doing to them-1 selves and their neighbours. At the same time, we have not power to force people to keep their butter at a low temperature, nor have we power to prevent this butter from being p'ut in the cold storage chambers. It may be that we ought to take that power

and it may be that parliament would give it to us. But, at present we have not that power. I have a pretty complete report of the season just past and also of that of a year ago. I have pointed out to the handlers and shippers of the butter how foolish their course was, and have begged them and encouraged them to do better, but I have not power to compel them to do better.
Did the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher) take any steps in consequence of the reports of the inspectors ?

I even went so far as to threaten, in the dairy conventions last winter, that if conditions did not improve during the season just past, I might have to ask parliament for this power of compulsion. I am glad to say that the reports of last season show an improvement-not so great as I would like, but still an improvement. I confess that I have hesitated to go to the extreme of asking parliament for the power to refuse admission to the cold storage chambers of goods under certain conditions. It would be going rather far. The steamship companies themselves would hesitate before agreeing that such power should be taken, because in certain seasons there is not enough freight to fill the cold storage chambers, and the companies are glad to get the goods, and they fake them. We bad this difficulty to contend with as well as with the carelessness of shippers in allowing their butter especially to get warmer than it ought to be. A considerable quantity of the butter brought to Montreal to be put in the cold storage chambers runs as high as fifty degrees, and 1 have no- hesitation in saying that butter cannot reach a temperature of fifty degrees without being harmed. It does reach that temperature, and at that temperature is put into the cold storage chambers, so that it must not merely be kept cool but actually cooled. That is one of the causes of variation in the recorded temperatures of the cold storage chambers. If you put a couple of hundred boxes of butter in a cold storage chamber at a temperature of say forty degrees when the temperature of the chamber ought to be. and is. twenty degrees, you raise the temperature of the chamber at once, and it will be a day, or perhaps two days, before the temperature can be brought down again to the proper level. As I have shown, the question is surrounded with difficulties. as hon. gentlemen will understand, and I confess that I have not been able to solve these difficulties completely.
Is the butter that comes in at a high temperature generally delivered as package freight in Montreal, or does it come on through shipment by rail?

Most of it, I think, comes by short-haul. That which comes from a long distance comes in refrigerator cars and
is generally fairly cool; but that which comes from a distance of one hundred miles or less from Montreal often does not come in refrigerator cars, although the cars are there, if the shippers would take advantage of them. But the great difficulty is in the carriage of butter from the creamery to the station and keeping it at the station for several hours, sometimes for half a day, before it is put in refrigerator cars. The refrigerator car cannot cool butter. If the butter is put in reasonably cool, the car will keep it so, but, with the refrigerator capacity they have they cannot reduce the temperature of the butter to any great extent. The railway and steamship companies say, with a good deal of justice, that it is not their business to cool the goods but only to keep them as cool as when they were put in. So, there is a good deal of difficulty in managing this trade. We have been trying to educate the people to their true interest and to get them to work the business to the best advantage, without using any absolute coercion.

Has the hon. minister conferred with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries with a view to establishing cold storage compartments in the new sheds which are being erected in Montreal, more especially .for the short-haul freight that he speaks of in the way of perishable goods?

I have not. I may say that in Montreal the cold storage accommodation provided by private concerns is fairly complete. There is no difficulty for people who ship goods on through bills of lading to have them arrive in Montreal .. day or two before they need to be put on the ships that they may be put in cold storage and properly cooled.
But I was speaking of the short-haul freight.
That appears to be the difficult question. But the goods can be very easily kept in the cold storage houses in Montreal and at a trifling expense.

I refer to the goods that are carried by shci t. railway haul and shipped directly to the steamer, and that do not go into cold storage in Montreal. Is provision being made for that business in connection with the new sheds?

Not that I am aware of. I have not had any representations made to me, either by the handlers of this produce or the shippers, asking for that. Of course that kind of thing would interfere with the business of cold storage warehouses in Montreal, there would be opposition to it. though I do not say it ought to succeed, if the arrangements are advisable. This question has been discussed by the trade to a certain extent, not particularly in connection with the new sheds in Montreal, but with the whole handling of goods. I may

say that in England most of the cold storage stores are on the docks and very convenient for handling. What I have seen ot them in England has led me to think they give satisfaction.

The tendency of the additional accommodation which is to be provided in the port of Montreal when the new improvements are completed, will be to create a larger amount of railway freight and a smaller quantity of local package freight. It will probably be necessary for the minister to make provision for cold storage accommodation on the wharfs themselves for the short haul railway freight that may be brought there.

There are some things that we ought to know before this passes. First, what is the temperature required and provided in the various chambers, and the capacity of these chambers for different kinds of fruit ? What is the proper temperature for carrying apples, pears, grapes, tomatoes, butter, cheese, meat and eggs ?
The officers of the department must know what is the proper temperature for carrying these various commodities. Then does the contract provide that there shall be suitable accommodation in these chambers, and sufficient capacity to carry the goods offered in those lines in chambers of the right temperature? Then, what will be the additional cost of freight on account of the cold storage they provide? I think we ought to have that information so as to enable us to understand whether the government has or has not made proper provision for cold storage in giving these subsidies to the steamship company.

The contract requires that they should provide cold storage to the satisfaction of the minister, with adequate space and at the different temperatures required. These are to be to the satisfaction of the minister. The vessels are running and I suppose the minister is perfectly satisfied with the facilities provided. The Allans, judging from their letter, prove that the facilities are adequate, and that whatever complaints have arisen they were not responsible for. That is where goods have been handed to them at a temperature higher than they should have been. I have before me a circular of one of the steamships, giving the space, one temperature of 30 degrees and another temperature of 20 degrees and a certain number of cubic feet. Shippers know what goods will go into the 30 degree compartment and what into the 20 degree compartment. There is no doubt that these points are fully guarded by the Minister of Agriculture. I do not know that the hon. gentleman himself can say that he has heard complaints with reference to freights. Of course, we could not govern the rates they charge for freights, I suppose they vary.
A few years ago the freight was to be so many shillings or so many cents above the ordinary rate on ves sels without cold storage.
A movable rate, but so much above.

There is one satisfaction in that information, and it is that we will know where to place the blame if we find out afterwards there is blame. From the information we have, there is blame, because the minister has just given us some information that our contract provides there shall be adequate cold storage according to the judgment of the Minister of Agriculture. If, therefore, the cold storage proves not to be adequate or suitable, then the Minister of Agriculture must be to blame, because he has an Inspector there to see that the goods are put on the vessel in proper condition and that the cold storage is provided as required.
I think the Minister of Agriculture will attend to the hon. gentlemen when his items come up.
What is the average speed of these vessels we have been paying for?

The 'Bavarian,' between Moville and Rimouski, a 17-knot steamer, 6 days during summer and 6i days in winter. The ' Tunisian ' and the ' Bavarian ' should not exceed 7 days in summer and days in winter.
I am not asking what they intend to do but what they have done.
They are not in service yet.
Those we had the con-ract with last year, what was their speed?
The contract is for 7i days in summer and 8 days in winter. They have complied with the contract.
You mean the contract is for a certain number of days, not for a certain number of knots?
Yes.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce gave us last year the speed of each vessel. I want to know the speed on the actual voyage.
I have not that with me.
Can't you give it within a knot or two? Is it 12 knots or is it 17 knots.? If I remember rightly, it was somewhere between 12 and 14, instead of 17.

These turbine steamers are about 17. The 'Tunisian' and 'Bavarian,' speaking from memory, average about 14 knots on the voyage.

Mr. HAGrGART. What is the speed of the others ?
The others would be slower, probably 10 or 12.

Will the minister be kind enough to have his clerk make out a list of the actual sailings of last year of each one of these vessels? What I want to get at is the actual speed they accomplish. We are paying $200,000 under this vote for what is called a fast line service, at least it is the fastest we have. Now, what is the real speed that has been accomplished? The minister last year, my colleague informs me, gave a table of these speeds. We may be getting an actual voyage service of 10 or 12 knots, or it may be 13, but it may not be as many knots as those knots I have spoken of indicate. But what we would like to know is how many knots we are getting, not how many days it took a boat to carry the minister over.
Will any of them x'each a higher rate of speed than the ' Minnie M.'?
