speechtext: Shall this item be carried ?
It is understood that we will get that information ?
The hon. gentleman will accept the statement that will be handed ir. to-morrow ?
Certainly.

To what extent do shippers avail themselves of cold storage for the transportation of their goods ? It is said by some-I do not know whether correctly or incorrectly-that the rates for cold storage were so high that many of the shippers decided to take the risk of sending their goods not in cold storage but in the ordinary way at the lower freight rate.
I am told by the lion. Minister of Agriculture that practically all of these shipments have gone by cold storage.
We have no information yet as to what the additional freight rates are to be over and above the movable rates. Have you provided for that in the contract ?
The rates are not controlled at all.
They were originally.
They were in the contract which I made when I subsidized vessels to induce them to put in cold storage. Those contracts were closed long ago and we have no further contracts.
Do you not think the government were derelict in their duty when they were giving steamships large subsidies if they did not provide for freight rates ?
Competition will regulate that.

We leave too many things to competition and we do not have competition afterwards. There is a great deal of complaint regarding it. The rates for shipment in cold storage were so high that a great many people thought it better to run the risk of their stuff spoiling.
Competition regulates that.

This is not competition. There seems to be an absence of business ability and astuteness on the part of the minister who makes this contract. It is failure on his part to make a suitable contract so as to secure the people who produce this stuff and the commercial men who ship it. In the interest of these producers and shippers it seems to me that something ought to be done; otherwise-they are at the mercy of every vessel on which they put their goods.

I will call the minister's attention to the suggestion.
Mr. FOSTER, What is the machinery for knowing that each one of these boats keeps the temperature at the required point during the whole voyage ? Have you an inspector on each vessel ?

There are self registering thermographs-generally two in each compartment.
Mr. FOSTER, And they are fixed at the commencement of the voyage and inspected at the end ?
Yes, they are locked by my officer in Montreal, taken out by my officer in Liverpool and sent back.
Is there no possibility of tampering with them ?
No.
Well, 'my officer' must have been sadly derelict in his duty last year because the information we got was that there were only a few on each vessel and that there were not two in each chamber.

Speaking from memory we have about 130 of these thermographs. Under ordinary circumstances they would serve our needs, but last year there was a large number of vessels fitted up with what is called cool storage. We did not know of that until the season was on and we could not get these thermographs in less than four months. They have to be made especially and we did not have enough of them in each of the chambers last year, both cold storage and cool storage, but they were put in just as rapidly as they could be got back. I think I may hazard a guess that eighty per cent of the chambers

of vessels which went out of Montreal were provided with thermographs.
It is rather an unsatisfactory way of providing for these things in a contract. Now, we are making a new contract. Has the hon. minister provided that there shall be enough thermographs this year ?
I have ordered more.
But the hon. minister knows the number of compartments these vessels contain.

I do not know at the present time how many vessels are going to run from Montreal with cold storage chambers.
Mr. 'SPROULE. But the hon. minister knows how many will get the government suosidies.
Yes.
Then I assume he knows the number of chambers he will require thermographs for ?
I guarantee my hon. friend that there will be a thermograph in every cold storage chamber in every vessel subsidized by the government.
Will the hon. minister see that thermographs are placed on the deck of the vessel so as to take the temperature of the sea air ?
We have not done that.
Is that not essential?

;My officers who have dealt with this matter have not thought so. I know that Mr. Smith brought that question forward and it was discussed, but my officers have not thought that is would be of any great value because the variations of the temperature on deck are so great that the instrument would hardly indicate them.
I am afraid the hon. minister's officers are hardly up to date as practical men.
In the contracts made with these vessels will there be any provision regarding freight rates ?
No.
It should be given out beforehand what the rates are to be so that shippers would know what they would have to pay for these cold storage chambers.
The contract is made and it is not in it. It is left to the regulation of trade competition.
The department has not shown good business ability.
We cannot regulate the price of commodities.

Is it of such little account that it is not worth while for the government to pay any attention to it ? AVhen we were told some years ago that it was an essential element of the contract that they should pay so much more if they availed themselves of this cold storage, shippers knew' whether it would be advis-Ftble for them to avail themselves of cold storage or not. Many shippers tell us that they did not avail themselves of cold storage because the rates were so high. The contract which was made by the old government or by the present government-I forget w'hftih- was nllow'ed to run out and w'as not renewed by this government. The South African war was on and freight rates went up. They said that they could not get the same freight rates and they did not provide for the equipment of these steamers until it was too late. Another year has elapsed since then. Have the government made no effort to get the freight rates fixed so that shippers may know where they stand? If not they have been derelict In their duty and they are censurable for their failure' Surely they ought to have made provision this year for freight rates. There is now no South African w'ar on and they ought to know that freight rates, let them be what they may, could easily have been provided for so that those availing themselves of cold storage w'ould not pay more than so many shillings or so many dollars or cents beyond the ordinary freight rate,
I will call the attention of the minister to the suggestion of the hon. gentleman.

Both last year and on previous occasions there has been some discussion upon items of this character as to alleged discrimination-it is called discrimination,* at least-as against Canadian shippers. The question arose in this way : It was alleged, with what truth I do not know, that upon some of these steamship lines-I do not say upon the lines of the Messrs. Allan-rates were given to shippers in the United States which were lower than those given from Canadian points of a corresponding inland distance. . That is to say, from Chicago, for example, you can get by some of the subsidized lines a lower rate for United States shippers than you can get for Canadian shippers from a point equally far west. Therefore, we complained with respect to some lines-I do not think there was any complaint with regard to the line of the Messrs. Allan-but with respect to some lines, which eventually resulted in a certain provision being inserted in some of these contracts with other steamship owners which forbade any such discrimination, if that is the term to use. The question was discussed during the past session, and, I think, during the session previous to that, and my recollection is that difficulties were fairly acknowledged On

both sides of the House. It was, of course, pointed out, I think by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on one occasion at least, that at Chicago these lines had to compete with lines running to New York, which had quite as good railway communication with Chicago as Montreal or St. John would have, and it was said that some ol' these owners could not avoid making offers ol' low rates where that was necessary for the purpose of competition. The Minister of Trade and Commerce last year, I think, promised us some further information on the subject, and I have no doubt that it has been under the consideration of my hon. friend the Minister of Customs before he undertook these estimates. I would be very glad indeed to know whether or not he has any information on the subject which he would like to impart to the committee, especially as to whether or not there have been any complaints made by shippers with regard to this particular line. I think we were told last year that there had been no complaint so far as this line was concerned.

I remember myself, not in connection with this, but 1 remember that two or three years ago a person wrote me from St. John charging that a subsidized line-I do not exactly remember the name, and therefore I will not mention it-were carrying goods cheaper from Boston than from St. John, although the boats were subsidized by this government from St. John. I understood from his complaint that they would bring the goods to St. John and then forward them to Boston, and yet, with this extra charge added, the rate was lower from Boston. I thought this was a matter that demanded attention, and I mentioned it to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. X think he immediately took steps to ascertain whether the charge was well founded or not. I presume there is not much in that, but I am told by the deputy that the question has arisen, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) has said, with reference to some large Chicago meat houses that were able to make a contract with every ship that went out giving them a very large consignment, and that under these circumstances-the Minister of Agriculture says that they were special cold storage chambers, not the cold storage chambers prepared by us, and that for these large shipments and steady sources of freight the Chicago houses were given better terms than were given to the shippers who were not able to offer the ship-owners as much freight at a time or as regular supplies. Otherwise, it is thought that the steamers would have gone with not half a load. I suppose that if they can get a full ship load they can afford to carry cheaper for the Canadian shipper in proportion than if they had only half a load.

There are, of course, considerations of that character which we
very frankly admitted should have weight with the government, but, at the same time, where we are paying out subsidies to a line such as this, or any other of these lines, it does seem a little incongruous that shippers in Canada should have to pay higher freights to such a subsidized line than the rates paid by shippers in the United States by the same line.
I am not sure whether there are complaints as to any of the subsidized lines ; they say there are none in reference to the Allan Line.

I understand there has been no complaint with regard to them. I know that last year the Minister of Trade and Commerce admitted it, and justified the action of certain steamship companies, and there was very considerable weight in what he said. He took the position that they could not get the freight unless they gave these lower rates, because these lower rates were given via New York, and that it was no injustice to the Canadian shipper, but indeed tended to maintain the line that the ship-owner should take the freight at these low rates. That was from the standpoint of the steamship-owner. From our standpoint it presented itself in this way. We were paying large subsidies to these ship-owners to maintain a line, and it seemed, as I said, incongruous that our own shippers should he paying more freight and higher freight rates than those paid by United States shippers.

Something like through and local freight by rail.
Mr. SPROULEi Has the government made any effort in the last year to develop the chilled meat or frozen meat trade ?
We have not taken any steps about it.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce made a promise to me for two or three successive years that he would furnish the House with a statement of the local rates and also the general rates by rail to Canadian ports and also the rates from Canadian inland points to foreign markets, and the American western rates to these same foreign markets. I have never heard of this information being laid on the table. I do not suppose it belongs to this department, but inasmuch as this question of subsidies to steamships is up, I think it would be well for the Minister of Customs, as a business man, to look into the matter, and have a guarantee that while the freights rates from western points over our lines and by our subsidized steamships to Britain might possibly be regulated so that while the long haul to western points might be reduced, yet in no case should the short haul, viz., to and frotrn Canadian points, be greater than the long haul. I

presume the minister knows, as every one knows, that the rates from Liverpool to Chicago or any western point are much lower than to our Canadian points.
Proportionately lower.

No ; actually lower. They can ship more cheaply say from (Belgium right into the western country west of the lakes than to points in Canada. I think it woud be a very proper thing for the minister to impress on his colleague-the Minister of Trade and Commerce is the one particularly interested -the necessity of having it enacted that no local rate should exceed in price the through rates.
Do you mean to make that a clause in the contract ?
In granting a subsidy, to provide that the local rate to a point in Canada should not exceed the through rate. I do not want it necessarily lower, but it should be as low.
I hope that the statement made by the hon. gentleman just now will induce him to assist me in compelling American roads to give the same rates to Canadian as to American shippers.
We do not control the American roads.

Last session the Minister of Trade and Commerce took an increased grant towards providing aids to navigation, especially, I think, in connection with the St. Lawrence. [DOT] He mentioned a system which could be installed in vessels which would give them notice when they were approaching shallow water, rocks, &c. It was some sort of telephonic arrangement under water. I would be glad to know if anything of that kind is being done in connection with these subsidized steamers. I think it is a matter of great importance, especially to steamers coming up the St. Lawrence in the summer months to Quebec or Montreal.

I do not feel at liberty to say that he has made a contract as to that, but I am warranted in saying that it has been seriously under consideration, and negotiations have been going on in reference to it.
I understood the minister to say that all the conditions of the contract made with the Allan Company have been performed. There have been no forfeitures ?
I think there have been no forfeitures.
I would like to know whether they have performed the provisions of the contract, or, if not, whether there has been an enforcement of the penalty.
No deductions have been made and therefore no penalties have been incurred.
That is not a consequence of the statement of the minister. A penalty may be incurred but not collected, and there may have been a forfeiture. I want to know whether there has been or not.

I am assured that the practice of the department has been, what I would expect it to be, that if there were any deductions to be made, they would be made at the time the cheque was given ; but that there have been no deductions, and therefore the full amount must have been earned.
Can the minister not state Whether the voyages have been performed according to the contract or not ?
Yes, and paid for.
Then, there is a new state of affairs this year as compared with last year, according to the statement then made by the minister.
I do not know what was stated last year. I am stating what I am informed by the deputy.
The minister will find on page 62 that $70,000 is provided for a submarine signal apparatus.
I think that is what the hon. member for St. John has been referring to.

On this item I would like to ask the hon. gentleman for some information. Where do we stand now in regard to the fast line ? When I left here we were in the bottle-necked business; where are we now ? Has there been any improvement in the communication between England and Canada ?

There has been a good deal of improvement. There are two turbine steamers going on in the spring which will make seventeen knots. They will make the crossing in six days in summer and six and a half days in winter.
With what companies have we contracts for carrying the mails between Canada and England 1
The Allan Line.
What is the contract price ?
Was that contract given after tenders had been asked from different companies ?

That is a contract made on November 7, 1903.
[Mr. BERGERON. Were tenders asked from different companies plying between Canada and England ?
I could not say.
What proportion of the Canadian mails are carried by Canadian vessels and what proportion through the United States ?
I gave the figures at the close of last session in reply to a question put to me by the hon. member for Centre Toronto.

This is a case in which it seems to me that we are spending a great deal of money for which we do not get benefit. Seven or eight years ago a contract was made by another administration for a fast line which would have carried not only our own mails, but probably a great part of the mails of the western states. The present government did not carry out that contract. Since then they have been insinuating that they were preparing a contract for a fast line, but it has never been carried to a successful issue. We are paying $260,000 a year or probably more for having our mails carried by a slow line; for in present conditions a line of fourteen or fifteen knots is a slow line. I know business men in Montreal to-day who send their mails through the United States instead of using the Canadian lines. There is no reason for that. Ivith the progressive government we have, and the growing times, when the supplies we are voting amount to about $65,000,000 compared with $35,000,000 or $40,000,000 eight or nine years ago, there is no reason why we should not have a Canadian line between Canada and England which would carry not only our own mails but the mails of the western states as well. It is the fault of the government if we have not a fast line to-day, and if we are obliged to delay the hon. gentleman's estimates by making these criticisms. I see the hon. minister looking at last year's Hansard, but I want something more fresh. I want information regarding what has happened since.

It is Impossible for me to give the weight of the mails carried since I spoke in this House in July last, but I shall be very happy to get the
information and give it to the hon. gentleman.
What I want to know is the proportion of mail matter carried by Canadian and American vessels?
I shall get the information and have it brought down on Tuesday or Wednesday next.
What is the arrangement about the steamers in winter time? Last year there was some change in the programme about calling at St. John and Halifax.
They call at Halifax in the winter en route for St. John.
What is the rule followed with regard to the sailing of all these subsidized steamers in winter time?
I will have that information when we are discussing the other item.
Last year the contract with the Allan Line was varied so that some of the sailings to St. John were cut out. Have those been restored?
I am not aware that any were cut out. Here is the contract.

Perhaps I may give both the minister and the hon. gentleman a little information on that point. The contract was not varied, but as a matter of fact the Allan steamers did not call at St. John on several of their trips. It was stated by their agent that they did not obtain freight with sufficient ease at St. John and it was thought they could do better by loading at Halifax. I remember speaking of this last session. My hon. friend will remember the hon. member for Annapolis, Mr. Wade, told us that the result of that experiment was that the steamers got barely enough freight in Halifax to give them steadiness in the sea-way, so that the experiment was not a success. This year they are loading at St. John. They always call at Halifax and leave their mails and generally passengers- not always all the passengers, generally the first class, but sometimes tne immigrants are brought on and landed at St. John. That is the way the contract is being carried out this year. They are calling at Halifax both ways, leaving the mails and passengers and finishing their voyage at St. John, where they get their freight.
That is very true, but, I understand they have the authority of the department for doing this.
The contract under which they are working now commenced in April last, and I am told they have been calling at both places since then.
Was there not another line of steamships that had a subsidy for carrying the mails?

The memorandum I have on this subject says that negotiations are under way for the establishment of this service, and definite announcement may be made before the House prorogues. The Postmaster General has been carrying on negotiations and no doubt can give any information any hon. members may desire.

The Mexican government has agreed with the Canadian government for a subsidized line of steamers on the Pacific and Atlantic. Last spring they agreed to go as high as $50,000, we doing the same. It was hoped that that amount would get us a line on the two oceans ; but when tenders were invited it was found that the whole amount would practically be absorbed by one line.
A monthly service ?

Yes. Last December I had negotiations with the Mexican government and they agreed, subject to our doing the same, that they would give another $50,000. This would mean a total of subsidies from two governments of $200,000, which would give us two lines, provided we could get them at that amount. But I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce is hardly likely to secure an Atlantic line for the sum here voted. The Mexican government will not give more than $50,000 extra, or $100,000 in all. It is probable that when the supplementary estimates are brought down the House may be asked to increase the subsidy. The amounts here voted will give us only the one line.
I think that the tenders show it would cost about $100,000 for the Pacific line-I cannot give the figures exactly.

Which would be the more expensive?
iSlr WILLIAM MULOCK. The Atlantic line.
What are the lines now?
Between Canada and Mexico there are none.
But between the United States and Mexico?
There is such a line but I do not recall the name.
Would this be given to a British or an American or to a Mexican line?
We were to advertise and the vessels were to carry the
British flag. The Mexican government have no ships carrying there flag.
Oh, yes.
The president of Mexico so informed me, and I suppose he ought to know.
How are the mails carried between Canada and Mexico?
They go through the United States.
What is the extent of the mails between Canada and Mexico?
There are no statistics to show that. This is not a matter of mails.
What w'ould be the ports of departure and call in Mexico and in Canada ?

In summer the vessels would leave Montreal and in winter some maritime province port or ports. They would call at a place called Progresso, the outport of Yucatan, which is part of the republic of Mexico. At Yucatan they raise great quantities of sisal fibre, which is used to mix with manila in the manufacture of binder twine. There would be a large import of this material, which at present we buy mainly in the New York market. The ship would then do some coasting and call at Coatzacoalcos, which is intended to be the gulf port of the Tehuantepec Railway, a railway crossing the peninsula from the Gulf of Mexico to the Pacific ocean. At present the only port that is available is Vera Cruz, but it is a good distance away and the Mexican government is at present making a harbour at Coatza-eoalcos. There will be a railway 196 miles across the peninsula to Salina Cruz, a harbour on the Pacific ocean now being improved by the Mexican government at very great expense. It is not in a backward state, and the contracts have been made for the expenditure of about $25,000,000 Mexican, which is about $12,000,000 gold. The next port would be Vera Cruz and then Tampico. That is connected with the interior of Mexico by a railway, just as Vera Cruz is. There are two railways going from Vera Cruz to the interior. So, if the Atlantic vessel were to call at each place it would be comparatively close to the interior of Mexico.

How long would it take a vessel to go from Montreal to the first port the hon. gentleman mentioned?
.Sir WILLIAM MULOCK. At what rate of speed?
If it were like the ' Gauss ' that came here from Germany, I suppose it would take seven months. But T mean an ordinary vessel of 14 knots.
I do not think you would put a cargo on a ship of 14 knots, it would be too expensive. I think it would be about 3,500 knots from Montreal to Vera Cruz.
Have you got a wharf there ?
No, you would have to use lighters.

How long does it take a vessel to go to these ports from New York ? The Minister of Customs says it is not so much a question of carrying mails as of bringing trade from Mexico to Canada. We do not want to pay $50,000 or $60,000 a year for a line of steamers which would not attain that object. If it takes a much longer time to carry the mails between Canada and Mexico by the proposed subsidized line, than to carry them by steamers plying between American ports and Mexican ports we would be throwing away our money, because our mails would go by the American line. Of course, if the hon. gentleman is not in a position to answer now, he can take means to obtain some statistics and bring them down.

I think the hon. gentleman has had his answer from the Minister of Customs. It is not a question of carrying mails at all. Under no circumstances would Canadian mails such as letters go by this line so long as they can go by rail. When you can go from Ottawa to the city of Mexico by rail in five days, letters will be carried by the shortest route. This proposition is for the development of trade for bulky articles of commerce that cannot afford to pay a large haul, but which may be transported a long distance by a cheaper route. I think there is a large market in the republic of Mexico that Canada can supply, and there is a reciprocal trade.
Would the hon. gentleman state what we might export there, and what we might import ?

As to imports, 1 mentioned a moment ago the article of sisal fibre. I think we consume in this country about 12,000,000 pounds of binder twine, into which sisal enters, I do not know in what proportion.
Worth how much ?

The raw material might be worth a cent and a half, perhaps, I do not know the price per pound. But it is a necessary article in Canada where we have a number of factories manufacturing binder twine. It is a growing industry, and we shall use more and more every year. We have to have that raw material. Canada does not produce it and Mexico does. Then coffee is grown in southern Mexico, tobacco, sugar and cotton. It 29
is an excellent country for growing raw cotton. As you are aware, grazing is carried on to a large extent in Mexico, and they export large quantities of hides of all kinds. In the mountains and central parts of Mexico where the country is rough, instead of sheep they have great flocks of goats, and the skins of goats are largely used in trade. I believe that is the raw material used in making fine leather. Then there are fruits. I do not know that we could do a banana trade, bananas being perishable. I think that trade is controlled by a company largely, and I do not think we would be able to do much in the banana trade. But we would be able to do something in many other fruits, oranges, lemons, nuts, cocoanuts, pineapples and so on. So far as our exports to Mexico are concerned, we could sell to them I think great quantities of Canadian products in the rough. We could sell them such things as coal on the Atlantic and on the Pacific. Mexico does not produce good coal to any extent. There are some coal deposits in the northeast part of Mexico, but they import great quantities of coal. Some of it comes in by rail into the northern parts, and portions of their coal are supplied from England and the United States by water. I think there is some continental coal also consumed'in Mexico. We ought also to be able to sell them pine. They have no white, pine in Mexico. We could sell them products of pine, such as household furniture and woodenware of various kinds. I was in conversation with a gentleman in the city of Mexico, who is a representative there of a Canadian house for boxes, which are shipped there in great quantities in what I think they call the knockdown state. Then there is a good market for railway ties. These are very valuable and very expensive. I was told by Mr. Brown, president of the National Railways that there would be no difficulty in marketing a million ties a year in Mexico, not to supply new roads but merely to make up the waste on existing roads. As to foods,
I am pleased to say that I found there a favourite cheese, the Imperial cheese. I believe we all know where that comes from.
Anything else imperial ?

Well, I am willing to admit-though I am not supposed to be an agent here for Canadian houses, but when the question is asked 'I am w'illing to admit that the first thing I saw when I entered the Buena Vista station-I am not making any confession, merely telling what I saw-but on leaving the Mexican Central station the first sign I saw' on reaching the street was on an establishment just opposite the station, and it was one of Walkers' advertisements-Canadian Club. I found on inquiry there was a house there which sold large quantities of that brand.
Did tlie hon gentleman find it the real article ?
That is a leading question.
We do not ask the hon. gentleman to incriminate himself.

I would not
know it even if I were to try it. My hon. friend will have to get an expert to answer that question. Then I am glad to say that we could sell them another article of food. My hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Mac-laren) would perhaps have some information on what I am about to say now. There is a very large wholesale and retail grocery establishment in the city of Mexico, and the enterprising owner of that House informed me that he sold large quantities of American Lams and bacons throughout Mexico in the city and elsewhere. He said that he only regretted that he could not get it in Canada and that he would be able to obtain the supplies from his own country-he is a native of our country-if we had a direct line of steamers. He is taking a great interest in this enterprise in the hope that this direct line of steamships may be the means of developing a trade of the kind I speak of. Butter is imported into Mexico in considerable quantities but it comes from France chiefly and it comes in tins. There is no reason why we should not capture the butter trade of Mexico if we put the goods up in the proper way and have proper transportation facilities. I was in conversation with a representative of some Toronto manufacturers and I found that a Toronto firm had captured the trade of the city of Mexico in what is known as neckwear. I do not know the details of that business, but I suppose it includes cravats, ties and so on. I also found that in the chief shops of the city of Mexico, Canadian leather goods were on sale in large quantities and that they came from establishments engaged in the manufacture of these goods in the city of loronto -such goods as trunks, pocket books, purses and small articles made of fine leather.
Gloves or anything of that kind ?

I did not happen to hear of those but there is no reason in the world why we should not get the glove trade to a large extent if our people are enterprising enough and we have the transportation facilities. But you cannot send anything like heavy freight by rail from here to Mexico. From where I am speaking now I suppose it would be nearly 3,000 miles by rail to the city of Mexico. That is a long distance to carry goods by land.
What is the trade today between Mexico and Canada ?
Practically nil.

I think if you turn up the Trade and Navigation returns of the republic of Mexico you will find that they are importing more and more every year. Speaking from memory-I may be wrong about this and I do not w'ant to be held to these figures, but I can give the statistics as I think I have some copies of their trade returns
Have they a high protective tariff ?

Yes, I think they import about $100,000,000. They are a growing and a coining people, and now is the time if we are going to get that trade before other countries get their lines of communication established. It is a very difficult thing to dislodge trade after it is once established. It is better to try and get it in its infancy.
The hon. minister was good enough to tell us that the president told him that they had no shipping.
No mercantile shipping.

Perhaps the president knows, but in going over Whittaker's Almanac and every other return given I find that they spend upwards of $2,000,000 in equipping their navy every year and that they have a mercantile marine of 23,817 tons.
Small coasting boats.
Even so.

They have no shipping in the sense of the subject we are discussing. The president informed me so and so did the Secretary of Finances, Mr. Limantour. They may have some small coasting vessels, but not ocean-going vessels such as are required for this traffic and they very readily assented to our controlling the flag.
That is what I wanted to make clear in the matter.
Yes.
Last year there was some talk of tenders being invited for this service. Will the hon. minister say what was done in connection with that ?

The Department of Trade and Commerce invited tenders. They only got one tender for the Pacific coast service and that was from Messrs. Weir & Co., of Glasgow. There were conditions coupled with it. The company sent a representative to Canada to try to obtain some modifications of the terms, and he left here intending to go to the city of Mexico to consult with the

Mexican government He has not returned to Canada yet and the Department of Trade and Commerce has not had any advice as to whether he has met with any success. As to the Atlantic coast service I think there was a tender from Messrs. Pickford & Black. The Elder Dempster Company did not put in a tender in answer to the advertisement but they are in negotiation with the department to see if they can make arrangements for that service.

Last year when this matter was before the House a gentleman (in Boston wrote me in reference to this service. He wanted to know what the department intended to do in the matter. I consulted with the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) but the information he gave me was so indefinite that it was of no use to the party in Boston. Therefore the matter dropped, as far as that firm was concerned. I understood from the indefinite way in which the hon. minister made his statement that the service they intended to establish was' a Pacific coast service and not an Atlantic service. That being the case these Boston parties had no further interest in it.

The first effort was for a Pacific coast service, but it is hoped, I believe, if the House sanctions it, that services may ultimately be established between Canada and the Mexican republic on both oceans.
But the present intention is only to establish a service on the Pacific coast ?

No, the Atlantic is more alive now than the Pacific. It started with the Pacific but obstacles presented themselves there. The representative of Andrew Weir & Co. who was here in connection with the contract on the Pacific coast, went to Mexico but he has not come back yet and it is at a standstill meanwhile.
What steps' did the department take to draw the attention of the public and of those interested in shipping to the contracts ?

Advertisements were inserted in the papers of the maritime provinces and then copies of these were sent to the High Commissioner with instructions to distribute them among the shipping ports of England.
Can the hon. minister tell us how much coal is shipped from the Pacific coast or from the eastern coast to Mexico ?

I have not looked up my trade and navigation returns. What about the thirty-nine items between the one we carried and this?
29*
Mr. f)ANIEL. I have some remarks on one or two of them.
Steam service between Halifax, St. John's, Newfoundland, and Liverpool, from July 1, 1905, to June 30, 1906, $20,000.
Who has that contract?
There is no change. Tlie date of the present contract is October 10, 1904, and it expires June 30, 1905. The contractors are Messrs. Furness, Withy & Co.	.
Is that a satisfactory service.
We have no complaints. The round trip is made in seventeen days.
I mean as far as the carrying trade is concerned.

We have no complaints and we therefore judge that it is satisfactory.
Steam service between St. John, N.B., and Glasgow, during winter of 1905-6, $15,000.

There is no change in that; the contractors are the Donaldson Line and the Robert Reford Line. They are paid $750 per round trip or $15,000 per annum and the carrying of mails is stipulated for.
Steam service between St. John, N.B., Dublin and Belfast during the winter of 1905-6, $7,500.

There is no change here. The date is October 20, 1904, and the contract expires with the opening of navigation, 1905. The contractors are the Ulster Steamship Company, the Head Line. The contractors have the privilege of calling at St. John's, Newfoundland, on the western trip. The subsidy is $750 each round trip. They carry mails but cold storage is not stipulated for.

In connection with this have the government taken any steps to have it made possible for these steamers to carry cattle? At the present time they cannot carry cattle even for slaughter on landing, because the British government will not allow cattle to be landed at any but certain few points even for slaughter. It would tend to increase trade to the old country, without detriment to British trade, If it were possible to allow these steamers to carry cattle.
We will look into that but if the policy of the British government is to prevent the landing
But the whole world centres around this government now and the government has only to wave its hand to have the matter attended to.

I think the hand should be waved.

A line or lines of steamers to run between St. John, Halifax and London, $10,000.

I would be glad if tlie minister would explain the present condition of this line and state the intention of the government with regard to asking for tenders. I may say that the Board of Trade of the city of St. John sent a memorial to the Governor General in Council with regard to this steamship service, with which I presume the minister is familiar. It was to the following effect :
That according to the records of the trade between St. John, Halifax and London which has been carried on for a number of years past by the Furness line of steamers subsidized by your government, the results have been extremely disappointing, more particularly in connection with the imports and exports of western Canadian goods (statements of which are inclosed herewith), in consequence of whch, and of the unsuitable and unsatisfactory steamers employed in the trade

Particulars concerning which I will also give directly.
*

there have been numerous strong complaints
on the part of both importers and exporters by the line ;
And whereas the Board of Trade has been informed by other responsible steamship companies, that they would be willing to tender for the service -commencing on 1st of July next, if allowed the opportunity of doing so ;
The St. John Board of Trade therefore respectfully requests that your government will, as soon as convenient, Issue a call for tenders for the following services to commence on 1st July next, viz. :-	.
A line or lines of steamers to run during the summer months between St. John, Halifax and London, and during the winter months between St John and London direct and Halifax and London direct, and that the steamship companies he allowed until the 1st April next for -submitting their tenders to the government.
(Signed) H. B. Schofield,
President.
With regard to the statement of the steamers referred to, I may say that when, this line was first subsidized, between 1S94 and 1900, the service was principally maintained by the following three steamers: The ' -St. John City,' and the ' Halifax City,' which were both new steamers, and the ' London City,' which was built in 1891, and therefore was only three years old at that time. They were good steamers but they were sold by the Furness Line, after which the service was carried on by the following inferior steamers: the ' Ulunda,' ' Madiana,'
' Dahome ' and ' Dalton Hall.' In November, 1900, the new steamer ' Evangeline ' came on, and In February, 1901, the new steamer ' Loyalist,' after which the service was maintained by the ' Evangeline,' 'Loyalist ' and ' Dahome.' -In January, 1902, the ' Evangeline ' and ' Loyalist ' were sold by the Furness Company, and the service has been carried on ever since with inferior steamers.

That is the statement of the Board of Trade, composed of merchants and shipping men well acquainted with this trade ; and I would like to ask if the communication which that board sent to the government has received any consideration, and whether it is the intention of the government to see that in future the company puts on such vessels as are competent to do in a satisfactory manner the work which it has contracted to do. The service has certainly not been satisfactory for the business men of St. John. T therefore take this opportunity of bringing this matter to the notice of the minister and to tell him that there are other shipping firms which are quite able and willing to tender for this service, and which would, in the opinion of the Board of Trade of the city of -St. John, carry it out in a more satisfactory manner than it appears to be done by the Furness Company under their present contract.
May I ask what is the date of that statement V And did 1 understand the hon. gentleman to say that a copy of it had been sent to the department ?
This copy does not give the date. The communication I got from the Board of Trade is dated January 20, 1905, and the letter of the president is dated January 19.

The deputy of the department has unfortunately been ill for some time, and lias not been able to give any assistance in preparing the information. The acting deputy is not aware that that memorandum has come to the department, but he has no doubt that it has from what the hon. gentleman has said. He has made a note of it, and the hon. gentleman may rely upon it being brought to the attention of the minister. There are two contracts running for those ports, one by the Canadian Pacific Railway Line and one by the Furness Line.
It is the Furness Line 1 am speaking of.

This Item had better stand, because there are other matters to be discussed in connection witli it.
Item allowed to stand.
Steam communication between St. John and Digby, from July 1, 1905, to June 30, 1906, $12,500.
I would like to ask the minister if the government have received any communication with regard to this line from the Maritime Board of Trade ?
Not that the acting deputy remembers.

Then I would like to read the following resolution which was passed at the annual meeting of the Maritime Board of Trade held at Moncton, N.B., on August 17, 1904.

Whereas, the increased requirements of commerce in the southwestern section of Nova Scotia, coupled with those of the Annapolis valley, demand greater transportation facilities and in particular a daily passenger and freight, service between St. John and Digby, N.S., whicti it is understood the Dominion Atlantic Railway Company will operate for a pro rata increase in the subsidy now paid.
Resolved, That the Maritime Board of Trade urge the federal government to provide daily steamboat communication between St. John and Digby by granting such pro rata increase in such subsidy ;
Further resolved. That as the four previous request's of this hoard for an improved hay service have been overlooked by the government, the present be submitted with the respectful request that it be dealt with immediately.
I may say that this Maritime Board of tirade is composed of business men of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. The hon. minister will notice that increased accommodation is asked for on behalf of several counties in the province of Nova Scotia. This service, I understand, is intended especially for the accommodation of those counties in Nova Scotia which border on the Bay of Fundy or which do business largely through the Bay of Fundy ports ; and if there were a better service between St. John and Digby, I think there is no doubt that the business would grow very greatly, and it would be a real boou to the people of those counties. I would be glad to know whether the matter has received any consideration from the government ; if so, what consideration it has received ; whether the government intend to act on the request of this memorial ; and, if so, how soon ?

The matter has been brought to the attention of the department, and is receiving their consideration. Under the present contract full round trips are made daily during June, July, August and September, four trips eacii week during October, November, December, March, April and May ; and three trips each week during January and February. If I apprehend it rightly, what the hon. gentleman read asks for a round trip daily all the year round.
Yes.

The contract has not been varied in that respect. It is dated June 1, 1904, and expires July 1, 1905, and is renewable for another year at the option of the minister. The minister, having that power, would I suppose, be able to take into consideration the wishes of the maritime board. He is not asking for a vote for that purpose just now ; but when he sees the remarks of the hon. gentleman and the expression of his belief that it would be beneficial, he may perhaps bring down a supplementary vote, though I cannot of course say anything about that.
Steam service between Victoria and San Francisco, $5,000.
This is an old item since confederation.

I believe the contract has expired and may not he taken up again. The original amount was $17,000, and was the result of an agreement entered into with the province of British Columbia when that province entered confederation.
We dropped that.

I am afraid not very effectively. It seems to he no good, commercially or otherwise.
From the information given me it would seem so.

My deputy thinks there might be a question as to whether we can drop it. If the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Foster) is right in saying that it was dropped, of course that would disprove that contention. Better let the item pass, and the minister will only make a contract if he finds it necessary.
Steam communication between Halifax and Newfoundland via Cape Breton ports, $2,000.
What ports does this take in ?

It is between Halifax and the west coast of Newfoundland, calling both coming and returning at St. Pierre, Grand Narrows, Baddeck, North and South Sydney and some other ports. I believe the contract has expired.
How many trips does the steamer make ?

A regular fortnightly service.
Steam communication during the- season of 1905, i.e., from the opening to the closing of navigation, between the mainland and the Magdalen Islands, $15,000.
What vessels are doing that ?

The steamers ' Amelia ' and ' Lunenburg.' Regular steam weekly service, making each week two full round trips. The contract expires on July 7th, 1908. It is with the Magdalen Island Steamship Company, Limited.

I would like to bring to the notice of the hon. minister another resolution with regard to steamship service with the Magdalen Islands, passed at the same meeting of the Maritime Board of Trade, held at Moncton, the 17th August, 1904. I do not know whether this resolution was formally sent to the government or not, but I presume it must have been :
Resolved, That the federal government be respectfully requested to grant a subsidy of $200 per trip for a steamer to make a weekly service between ports on the north side of Prince Edward Island, Miramichi, Magdalen Island and North Sydney, the distance on the whole route being about 625 miles.
I am not in a position to advocate the matter very strongly, because I am not so familiar with the ports on the north side of Prince Edward Island as are the members from that province. Perhaps the hon. member for Queen's will be able to give us a little information on this matter, but I take this opportunity of bringing this resolution before the minister, in order that he may give it his consideration.
